locales:
  ru:
    title: Чем SpinLock и SpinWait отличаются от lock на основе Monitor и когда ожидание в цикле окупается?
    prompt: |
      Чем `SpinLock` и `SpinWait` отличаются от обычного `lock`, который в .NET 10 для объекта типа `object` работает
      через `Monitor`? В каких условиях активное ожидание в цикле (spinning) действительно выгоднее блокировки потока,
      и как вы решите, стоит ли заменять `lock` на `SpinLock` в конкретном месте?
    hint: Во что обходится ожидающий поток в каждом случае и насколько коротким должно быть ожидание, чтобы одна из этих цен оказалась меньше?
    answer: |
      **Что делает каждый примитив.**

      - `lock` / `Monitor`: реентерабельная блокировка с владельцем-потоком. При конкуренции среда выполнения сначала
        недолго крутится в цикле в надежде, что владелец скоро освободит блокировку, а если не дождалась, поток засыпает
        на объекте ожидания ОС и отдаёт ядро. Пробуждение стоит переключения контекста, зато спящий поток не тратит
        процессор. Есть `Monitor.Wait` / `Monitor.Pulse`. С .NET 9 есть и тип `System.Threading.Lock`: `lock` по полю
        этого типа использует его, и устроен он по той же схеме "сначала покрутиться, потом заблокироваться".
      - `SpinLock`: структура с методами `Enter(ref bool lockTaken)`, `TryEnter` и `Exit`. Она не реентерабельна:
        повторный `Enter` в том же потоке при включённом отслеживании владельца выбрасывает `LockRecursionException`,
        а при выключенном - приводит к взаимной блокировке. Ожидающий поток не засыпает на объекте ядра: он крутится
        в цикле, а по мере роста числа попыток уступает квант времени, но продолжает опрашивать блокировку. Нет
        `Wait` / `Pulse`, нет справедливости очереди.
      - `SpinWait`: не блокировка, а помощник для цикла ожидания. `SpinOnce` сначала выполняет короткое активное
        ожидание на уровне процессора, а после нескольких итераций переходит к уступке кванта; на однопроцессорной
        машине он всегда уступает квант. `NextSpinWillYield` подсказывает, когда крутиться уже бессмысленно,
        а `SpinWait.SpinUntil(condition, timeout)` ждёт выполнения условия. Его используют для своих неблокирующих
        алгоритмов и двухфазного ожидания "покрутиться, затем заблокироваться" (так устроен, например,
        `ManualResetEventSlim` со свойством `SpinCount`).

      **Когда ожидание в цикле окупается.** Нужны все условия сразу:

      1. Критическая секция очень короткая: несколько десятков или сотен инструкций, без выделения памяти, ввода-вывода,
         вызовов, которые могут заблокироваться, и виртуальных вызовов в незнакомый код. Ожидание должно быть короче,
         чем стоят усыпление и пробуждение потока (переключение контекста - порядка микросекунд).
      2. Владелец блокировки прямо сейчас выполняется на другом ядре: машина многоядерная, конкурирующих потоков не
         больше, чем ядер. Если владельца вытеснил планировщик или приостановил сборщик мусора, ожидающие сжигают
         свои кванты впустую.
      3. Конкуренция низкая: блокировка обычно свободна или освобождается почти сразу. При высокой конкуренции
         множество крутящихся потоков тратят процессор и мешают владельцу (перекидывание строки кэша между ядрами).
      4. Блокировок много и они мелкие (например, по одной на узел структуры данных), и важно, что `SpinLock` -
         структура без отдельного объекта в куче.

      **Почему `SpinLock` выигрывает редко.** `Monitor` уже крутится короткое время перед блокировкой, поэтому
      для коротких и слабо конкурентных секций он и так почти не уходит в ядро. Заметная разница появляется только
      в узких случаях из списка выше. Поэтому порядок такой: начать с `lock`, а на `SpinLock` переходить только после
      измерений - бенчмарка (BenchmarkDotNet) при реалистичной конкуренции и данных из production (счётчик
      конкуренции `Monitor.LockContentionCount`, загрузка процессора). Часто выгоднее вообще снизить конкуренцию:
      укоротить секцию, разделить данные на сегменты, использовать `Interlocked`, конкурентные коллекции или
      неизменяемые снимки.

      **Ловушки `SpinLock`.**

      - Это изменяемая структура: копия - это отдельная блокировка. Передавайте её по `ref`, не храните в поле
        `readonly` (вызов `Enter` пойдёт на защитной копии) и не прячьте в автосвойство.
      - Отслеживание владельца удобно для отладки, но стоит времени; его отключают через конструктор
        `new SpinLock(false)`.
      - Внутри нельзя блокироваться, ждать другие блокировки и делать долгую работу: ожидающие потоки всё это время
        тратят процессор. В контейнере с лимитом CPU это ещё и съедает квоту и приводит к троттлингу.
      - Шаблон использования: `bool lockTaken = false; try { spinLock.Enter(ref lockTaken); ... } finally { if (lockTaken) spinLock.Exit(); }`.
    explanation: |
      Это выбор между двумя ценами. Блокировка потока стоит двух переключений контекста (усыпить и разбудить), но
      освобождает ядро для другой работы. Активное ожидание стоит процессорного времени, пропорционального длине
      ожидания. Крутиться выгодно, только если ожидаемое время ожидания меньше цены блокировки, а это верно лишь
      для очень коротких секций при низкой конкуренции и при владельце, который выполняется на другом ядре.
      `Monitor` в .NET 10 страхует оба случая: короткое ожидание проходит в цикле, длинное - на объекте ОС.

      Слабый ответ - "`SpinLock` быстрее, потому что не обращается к ядру". Без измерений он легко оказывается
      медленнее: под конкуренцией или при вытеснении владельца ожидающие сжигают ядра, а `Monitor` к тому моменту уже
      уступил бы процессор. Сильный ответ объясняет экономику ожидания, называет условия и требует измерений перед
      заменой. Описание относится к .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - SpinLock (обзор)
      - Структура SpinWait
      - Структура SpinLock
  en:
    title: How do SpinLock and SpinWait differ from a Monitor-based lock, and when does spinning pay off?
    prompt: |
      How do `SpinLock` and `SpinWait` differ from an ordinary `lock`, which in .NET 10 works through `Monitor` for an
      object of type `object`? Under which conditions is busy waiting in a loop (spinning) really better than blocking
      the thread, and how would you decide whether to replace `lock` with `SpinLock` in a specific place?
    hint: What does a waiting thread cost in each case, and how short must the wait be for one of these costs to be the smaller one?
    answer: |
      **What each primitive does.**

      - `lock` / `Monitor`: a reentrant lock owned by a thread. Under contention the runtime first spins for a short
        while, hoping that the owner releases the lock soon, and if that does not happen, the thread sleeps on an OS
        wait object and gives up the core. Waking up costs a context switch, but a sleeping thread burns no CPU.
        `Monitor.Wait` / `Monitor.Pulse` are available. Since .NET 9 there is also the `System.Threading.Lock` type:
        `lock` on a field of that type uses it, and it follows the same "spin first, then block" scheme.
      - `SpinLock`: a struct with `Enter(ref bool lockTaken)`, `TryEnter` and `Exit`. It is not reentrant: a repeated
        `Enter` on the same thread throws `LockRecursionException` when owner tracking is enabled, and deadlocks when
        it is disabled. A waiting thread never sleeps on a kernel object: it spins, and as the number of attempts grows
        it yields its time slice, but it keeps polling the lock. There is no `Wait` / `Pulse` and no fair queue.
      - `SpinWait`: not a lock but a helper for a wait loop. `SpinOnce` first does a short busy wait at the CPU level,
        and after a few iterations switches to yielding the time slice; on a single-processor machine it always yields.
        `NextSpinWillYield` tells you when spinning stops being useful, and `SpinWait.SpinUntil(condition, timeout)`
        waits for a condition. It is used for your own lock-free algorithms and for two-phase waits "spin, then block"
        (this is how, for example, `ManualResetEventSlim` with its `SpinCount` property works).

      **When spinning pays off.** All conditions are needed at once:

      1. The critical section is very short: tens or hundreds of instructions, with no allocations, no IO, no calls
         that can block and no virtual calls into unknown code. The wait has to be shorter than the cost of putting
         a thread to sleep and waking it up (a context switch is on the order of microseconds).
      2. The lock owner is running on another core right now: the machine has several cores and there are no more
         contending threads than cores. If the scheduler has preempted the owner, or the garbage collector has
         suspended it, the waiters burn their time slices for nothing.
      3. Contention is low: the lock is usually free or released almost at once. Under high contention many spinning
         threads waste CPU and slow down the owner (a cache line bouncing between cores).
      4. There are many fine-grained locks (for example, one per node of a data structure), and it matters that
         `SpinLock` is a struct with no separate heap object.

      **Why `SpinLock` rarely wins.** `Monitor` already spins for a short time before blocking, so for short, lightly
      contended sections it hardly ever goes to the kernel anyway. A visible difference appears only in the narrow cases
      above. So the order is: start with `lock`, and move to `SpinLock` only after measuring - a benchmark
      (BenchmarkDotNet) under realistic contention and production data (the `Monitor.LockContentionCount` contention
      counter, CPU usage). Often it is better to reduce contention instead: shorten the section, shard the data, or use
      `Interlocked`, concurrent collections or immutable snapshots.

      **`SpinLock` pitfalls.**

      - It is a mutable struct: a copy is a separate lock. Pass it by `ref`, do not store it in a `readonly` field
        (the `Enter` call would run on a defensive copy), and do not hide it behind an auto-property.
      - Owner tracking helps debugging but costs time; it is turned off with the `new SpinLock(false)` constructor.
      - Inside it you must not block, wait for other locks or do long work: the waiting threads burn CPU the whole
        time. In a container with a CPU limit this also eats the quota and leads to throttling.
      - The usage pattern: `bool lockTaken = false; try { spinLock.Enter(ref lockTaken); ... } finally { if (lockTaken) spinLock.Exit(); }`.
    explanation: |
      This is a choice between two costs. Blocking a thread costs two context switches (put it to sleep and wake it up)
      but frees the core for other work. Spinning costs CPU time proportional to the length of the wait. Spinning wins
      only when the expected wait is shorter than the cost of blocking, and that holds only for very short sections with
      low contention and an owner that is running on another core. `Monitor` in .NET 10 hedges both cases: a short wait
      is handled by spinning, a long one by an OS wait object.

      A weak answer is "`SpinLock` is faster because it does not go to the kernel". Without measurements it easily turns
      out slower: under contention, or when the owner is preempted, the waiters burn cores, while `Monitor` would already
      have given up the CPU. A strong answer explains the economics of waiting, names the conditions and demands
      measurements before the switch. The description refers to .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - SpinLock (overview)
      - SpinWait struct
      - SpinLock struct

    public sealed class BoundedBuffer<T>
    {
        private readonly object _gate = new();
        private readonly Queue<T> _items = new();
        private readonly int _capacity;

        public BoundedBuffer(int capacity) => _capacity = capacity;

        public void Add(T item)
        {
            lock (_gate)
            {
                while (_items.Count == _capacity)
                {
                    Monitor.Wait(_gate);
                }
                _items.Enqueue(item);
                Monitor.PulseAll(_gate);
            }
        }

        public T Take()
        {
            lock (_gate)
            {
                while (_items.Count == 0)
                {
                    Monitor.Wait(_gate);
                }
                T item = _items.Dequeue();
                Monitor.PulseAll(_gate);
                return item;
            }
        }
    }

  en:
    title: What does Monitor.Wait do with the lock, and why check the condition in a while loop?
    prompt: |
      A bounded buffer for a producer-consumer scheme is built on `lock` and `Monitor.Wait`/`Monitor.PulseAll`.
      Several producers call `Add`, several consumers call `Take`.

      What does `Monitor.Wait(_gate)` do with the `_gate` lock, and why is the wait condition checked in a `while` loop
      rather than in an `if`?
    hint: How could a producer ever enter `lock (_gate)` and call `PulseAll` while a consumer is inside `Wait`? And what can other threads do between the signal and the moment `Wait` returns?
    options:
      a: "`Wait` releases the lock, waits for a `Pulse`/`PulseAll` signal and reacquires the lock before returning. Between the signal and the reacquisition another thread can take the lock and change the state, so the condition has to be rechecked in a loop"
      b: "`Wait` keeps holding the lock while the thread sleeps, and the `while` loop is needed because a `Pulse` signal is sometimes lost and the wait has to be repeated"
      c: "`Wait` releases the lock and returns without reacquiring it, so the code after `Wait` runs outside the lock, and `while` instead of `if` is only a matter of style"
      d: "`Wait` releases the lock, and `PulseAll` atomically hands it to the woken thread, so after `Wait` returns the condition is guaranteed to hold and an `if` would be enough"
    optionExplanations:
      b: "If the waiting thread kept the lock, no producer could enter `lock (_gate)` and call `PulseAll`: the result would be a deadlock. Releasing the lock for the duration of the wait is the whole purpose of `Wait`."
      c: "`Wait` returns only after the thread owns the lock again. Otherwise `Dequeue` would run without synchronization, and leaving the `lock` would call `Monitor.Exit` on a lock the thread does not own. And `while` here is not style but a correctness requirement."
      d: "`PulseAll` only moves the waiting threads to the ready queue. The lock stays with the calling thread until it leaves its `lock`, and then all ready threads compete for it together with new threads entering `lock`. Another consumer can get there first and take the item."
    answer: "`Wait` releases the lock, waits for a signal and reacquires the lock before returning; meanwhile other threads may have changed the state, so the condition is rechecked in a `while` loop."
    explanation: |
      `Monitor.Wait(_gate)` may only be called while owning the `_gate` lock, otherwise `SynchronizationLockException` is thrown.
      The call releases the lock and puts the thread into the object's waiting queue. `Pulse` or `PulseAll` moves a waiting
      thread to the ready queue, but the thread does not get the lock yet: it stays with the signalling thread until that
      thread leaves its `lock`. Then the woken thread competes for the lock with other threads and returns from `Wait` only
      once it owns the lock again.

      Between the signal and the return from `Wait`, another thread can take the lock first: a second consumer woken by the
      same `PulseAll`, or a thread that has just entered `Take`. It takes the item, and the queue is empty again. That is why
      the condition is checked again after `Wait` returns: `while`, not `if`. With `if` a consumer would call `Dequeue` on an
      empty queue and get `InvalidOperationException`, and a producer would exceed the buffer capacity.

      There is a second reason. Producers and consumers wait on the same object, `PulseAll` wakes all of them, and the woken
      thread may have been waiting for a different condition. A single `Pulse` is dangerous in this scheme: it can wake a
      thread of the wrong kind, and the signal is effectively lost. Also, `Monitor` does not remember a `Pulse` when nobody
      is waiting at that moment, so waiting is always tied to checking the state under the lock, not to the signal itself.

      In practice such a buffer is rarely written by hand: there are `BlockingCollection<T>` and `Channel<T>`. The behaviour
      of `Monitor` is the same in all .NET versions, including .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - Monitor.Wait method
      - Monitor class

fixedSource: |
  using System.Text;

  Stack<StringBuilder> pool = new();

  StringBuilder Rent()
  {
      return pool.Count > 0 ? pool.Pop() : new StringBuilder();
  }

  void Return(StringBuilder builder)
  {
      builder.Clear();
      pool.Push(builder);
  }

  string FormatMessage(string user, int unread)
  {
      StringBuilder builder = Rent();
      try
      {
          builder.Append(user).Append(": ").Append(unread).Append(" unread");
          return builder.ToString();
      }
      finally
      {
          Return(builder);
      }
  }

  Console.WriteLine(FormatMessage("alice", 3));
  Console.WriteLine(FormatMessage("bob", 5));

      Программа должна вывести `alice: 3 unread`, а затем `bob: 5 unread`, но на .NET 10 вторая строка выглядит так:
      `alice: 3 unreadbob: 5 unread`. Исключения нет. Щёлкните по строке с дефектом.
    hint: В каком состоянии объект попадает обратно в пул и что с ним застаёт следующий, кто его возьмёт?
    answer: "Строка 12: `Return` кладёт `StringBuilder` в пул как есть, не вызвав `builder.Clear()`, поэтому следующий арендатор дописывает текст к содержимому предыдущего."
    explanation: |
      Первый вызов `FormatMessage` не находит объектов в пуле, создаёт новый `StringBuilder`, записывает в него
      `alice: 3 unread` и в `finally` возвращает его в пул. `Return` просто делает `Push`, и вместе с объектом в пул уходит
      весь накопленный текст. Второй вызов получает этот же экземпляр из `Pop`, а `Append` дописывает в конец, поэтому
      `ToString()` возвращает `alice: 3 unreadbob: 5 unread`. Пул ничего не знает о состоянии объекта, он только хранит ссылки.

      Правило пулинга: объект, который возвращают в пул, должен быть приведён в исходное состояние, иначе пул раздаёт
      «грязные» объекты. Для `StringBuilder` это `Clear()`: метод удаляет все символы (то же самое, что `Length = 0`),

      при аренде: объект не хранит в пуле чужие данные (а они могут быть чувствительными), и в этом же месте удобно решить,
      стоит ли вообще оставлять объект, например выбросить сильно разросшийся буфер, чтобы пул не держал лишнюю память.

      однопоточного кода; в общем случае лучше взять готовый `ObjectPool<T>`.

    title: Find the line that makes a StringBuilder from a hand-written pool mix in text from the previous message
    prompt: |
      To avoid creating a `StringBuilder` for every message, the code keeps them in a simple pool built on `Stack<StringBuilder>`.
      The program should print `alice: 3 unread` and then `bob: 5 unread`, but on .NET 10 the second line reads
      `alice: 3 unreadbob: 5 unread`. No exception is thrown. Click the line that contains the defect.

    explanation: |
      The first `FormatMessage` call finds no objects in the pool, creates a new `StringBuilder`, writes
      `alice: 3 unread` into it and returns it to the pool in `finally`. `Return` only calls `Push`, so all the accumulated
      text goes into the pool together with the object. The second call gets the same instance from `Pop`, and `Append`
      writes at the end, so `ToString()` returns `alice: 3 unreadbob: 5 unread`. The pool knows nothing about the object's
      state; it only stores references.

      The pooling rule: an object returned to a pool must be reset to its initial state, otherwise the pool hands out
      "dirty" objects. For `StringBuilder` that is `Clear()`: it removes all characters (the same as `Length = 0`) but
      keeps the already allocated buffer, which is the whole reason for the pool. Resetting on return is better than on
      rent: the object does not keep someone else's data while it sits in the pool (and that data may be sensitive), and
      the same place is convenient for deciding whether to keep the object at all, for example to drop a buffer that has
      grown too large so the pool does not hold on to extra memory.

      The ready-made pool from the `Microsoft.Extensions.ObjectPool` package works the same way: the
      `StringBuilderPooledObjectPolicy` clears the `StringBuilder` in its `Return` method and refuses to keep instances whose
      capacity has exceeded a configured limit. Also, `Stack<T>` is not thread-safe, so a hand-written pool like this one is
      only suitable for single-threaded code; in general, prefer the ready-made `ObjectPool<T>`.

      - StringBuilder.Clear method
      - Object reuse with ObjectPool in ASP.NET Core

  en:
    title: What happens to a frequently read IMemoryCache entry that has only SlidingExpiration set?
    prompt: |
      A .NET 10 service caches a product price in `IMemoryCache` with only a `SlidingExpiration` of 5 minutes. The price
      of a popular product is requested several times a second. An administrator changes the price in the database, and
      the code that writes to the database does not touch the cache. What happens to the cache entry?
    hint: From what moment is a sliding interval measured, and what restarts it?
    options:
      a: The entry expires 5 minutes after it was created, and the next request loads the new price from the database
      b: Every read restarts the 5-minute interval, so the entry never expires and the service serves the old price indefinitely
      c: "`MemoryCache` tracks changes in the data source and removes the entry itself once the price in the database is updated"
      d: Every 5 minutes the cache calls the factory again in the background and so refreshes the price
    optionExplanations:
      a: That is how an absolute lifetime (`AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow`) behaves. A sliding interval is measured not from the creation of the entry but from the last access to it.
      c: "`MemoryCache` knows nothing about the data source. An entry is removed only when its expiration passes, by an explicit `Remove` call, when an attached change token fires, or by eviction under a configured size limit."
      d: "`MemoryCache` has no background refresh of values. The factory in `GetOrCreateAsync` runs only on a miss, that is, when the entry is not in the cache."
    answer: Every read restarts the 5-minute interval, so the entry never expires and the service serves the old price indefinitely.
    explanation: |
      `SlidingExpiration` means "remove the entry if nobody accessed it within the interval". Every successful read
      (`TryGetValue`, `Get`, `GetOrCreateAsync` with a hit) updates the last access time, and the countdown starts over.
      If the entry is read more often than once every 5 minutes, the interval never runs out. The ASP.NET Core
      documentation warns about this directly: an entry with only a sliding expiration is at risk of never expiring.

      As a result the old price stays in the cache until the entry is removed explicitly, evicted by a size limit, or
      the process restarts. The worst part is that this hits exactly the most popular entries: rarely read products get
      refreshed, hot ones do not.

      The fix is to cap the lifetime: set an absolute expiration together with the sliding one, for example
      `entry.AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30)`. The entry is then removed as soon as either of
      the two expirations passes, and the absolute one sets the maximum staleness of the data. If a stale price is not
      acceptable at all, the code that changes the price should also call `cache.Remove(key)` (or use a change token).
      The behaviour is described for .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - Cache in-memory in ASP.NET Core
      - MemoryCacheEntryOptions.SlidingExpiration property

  en:
    title: Which lines of a hot C# loop allocate on the managed heap on every iteration?
    prompt: |
      The `Run` method is called on a hot path with a large `iterations`. The lines are marked with the comments `A`-`E`.
      Select all lines that, by the semantics of C# 14 and .NET 10, request an allocation on the managed heap on
      **every** iteration of the `for` loop. Ignore JIT compiler optimizations that might remove allocations.
    hint: Look at the static type of the expression each `foreach` iterates, and at what each lambda needs to remember from the surrounding code.
    options:
      a: "`A`: `foreach` over the variable `list` of type `List<int>`"
      b: "`B`: `foreach` over the variable `sequence` of type `IEnumerable<int>`, which refers to the same list"
      c: "`C`: `list.Exists` with a lambda that uses the local variable `limit`"
      d: "`D`: `list.Exists` with the lambda `x => x < 0`, which captures nothing"
      e: "`E`: the interpolated string assigned to `key`"
    optionExplanations:
      a: "For an expression of type `List<int>` the compiler finds the public `GetEnumerator` method, which returns the struct `List<int>.Enumerator`. The enumerator lives in a local variable, nothing is boxed, and the `foreach` allocates nothing on the heap."
      d: "The lambda captures no locals and no `this`, so the compiler caches the delegate in a static field of a hidden class. The delegate is created once, on the first execution, and later iterations take it from the cache. `List<T>.Exists` itself walks the internal array and allocates nothing either."
    answer: "`b`, `c` and `e` are correct: boxing the enumerator in a `foreach` through an interface, a closure with a new delegate when `limit` is captured, and a new string from the interpolation. Lines `A` and `D` allocate nothing in the steady state."
    explanation: |
      - **`A` - no allocation.** `foreach` first looks for a suitable `GetEnumerator` method on the static type of the
        expression. `List<T>.GetEnumerator()` returns the struct `List<T>.Enumerator`, so the enumerator is kept as a local
        variable, not on the heap.
      - **`B` - boxing.** The static type of `sequence` is `IEnumerable<int>`, so the compiler calls the interface method
        `IEnumerable<int>.GetEnumerator()`, which returns `IEnumerator<int>`. The struct `List<int>.Enumerator` has to be
        boxed, so every execution of this `foreach` creates one heap object. Parameters and fields of type
        `IEnumerable<T>`, and most LINQ operators, have the same effect.
      - **`C` - a closure.** The variable `limit` is declared inside the loop body, so on every iteration the compiler
        creates a new instance of a hidden class (the closure) that holds it, and a new `Predicate<int>` delegate bound to
        that instance. That is two allocations per iteration.
      - **`D` - no allocation.** A non-capturing lambda becomes a method of a hidden class, and the compiler creates the
        delegate to it once and caches it in a static field.
      - **`E` - a new string.** Since C# 10 interpolation goes through `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler`: the `int` is
        formatted without boxing and the temporary buffer comes from a pool. But the result is a new `string` object, and
        it is created on every iteration.

      A caveat for .NET 10: in some cases the JIT can use escape analysis to place small objects on the stack and so remove
      some of these allocations. That is an optimization, not a language guarantee, and a hot path must not rely on it.
      Measurement shows the real picture, for example the `Allocated` column of `[MemoryDiagnoser]` in BenchmarkDotNet or
      an allocation profiler.
    linkTitles:
      - List<T>.GetEnumerator method
      - Iteration statements (foreach)
      - String interpolation

  en:
    title: "Users say the product is slow, there are no performance requirements, and every developer wants to optimize something different: what does the lead do?"
    prompt: |
      Users and the sales team complain that the product is "slow". There are no formal performance requirements.
      At a meeting every developer proposes optimizing their own area: one wants to rewrite serialization, another to
      add a cache, a third to move the code to `Span<T>`. What do you do as the lead, and in what order?
    hint: How will the team know that the performance work is finished, and by what criterion do you pick where to start?
    answer: |
      1. **Turn complaints into data.** Find out which user scenarios are slow, for whom and since when. Look at what
         production already reports: latency per endpoint or operation as percentiles, error rate, throughput. If there
         is no such telemetry, adding it is the first task. For a quick look at a running process, `dotnet-counters`
         shows CPU usage, garbage collector activity, thread pool queue length and exception rate without restarting the
         application.
      2. **Agree on a measurable goal.** Together with the product owner, fix a target for the key scenarios, for example
         "p95 of order search under 400 ms at 200 requests per second", and the load profile it applies to. Percentiles,
         not averages: an average hides the slow tail that users complain about. The goal tells the team when to stop.
      3. **Capture a baseline.** Reproduce the load in an environment close to production and record the present
         numbers, so every change is compared against the same reference point.
      4. **Find the largest contributor.** First split the request time by component with distributed tracing: database,
         external calls, application code, waiting in queues. Then go deeper where the time is: `dotnet-trace` for CPU and
         wait profiles, `dotnet-counters` for the garbage collector and thread pool starvation, `dotnet-dump` for hangs.
         Collect the developers' ideas into one list and rank them by measured share of time and cost of the fix.
      5. **Fix the top item and re-measure.** One change at a time, checked against the baseline and the goal under the
         same load. If the goal is met, stop and move the remaining ideas to the backlog. If not, profile again: the
         bottleneck has moved.
      6. **Keep it from coming back.** A load check or benchmark of the key scenarios in the pipeline or on a schedule,
         a dashboard and an alert on the p95 target in production, and the target itself written down as a
         non-functional requirement for further features.
      7. **Lead the team through it.** Explain the plan, give the people with optimization ideas the profiling tasks,
         time-box the investigation, and settle disagreements with measurements instead of opinions.
    explanation: |
      Optimizing without a goal and without a profile spreads effort over code that may not affect what users see at
      all. This is Amdahl's law: if a component takes 5% of the request time, even making it infinitely fast cuts the
      time by at most 5%. Intuition about "hot spots" is often wrong: a slow page may barely use the CPU and instead wait
      for the database, an external service or a lock, and then faster serialization changes nothing.

      A measurable goal turns "slow" into an engineering task with a definition of done. It gives arguments for
      prioritization in conversations with the business and lets the team decline optimizations that do not pay off.
      A regression check is needed because performance usually degrades gradually, feature by feature, and without
      automated control it drifts back to where it started within a few releases. The tools are described for .NET 10:
      `dotnet-counters` is meant for first-level monitoring of a process's health, `dotnet-trace` for detailed profiling
      once you know which process and scenario to investigate.
    linkTitles:
      - .NET diagnostics tools overview
      - dotnet-counters tool
      - dotnet-trace tool

  en:
    title: How do you catch performance regressions in CI when benchmark results on shared runners vary by 20%?
    prompt: |
      The team added BenchmarkDotNet benchmarks to CI to catch performance regressions before merging. CI runs on shared
      cloud runners, and the same unchanged code shows up to 20% difference in time between runs. Builds turn red and
      green for no reason, and developers start ignoring the result. As the lead, which approach do you propose to the team?
    hint: Which part of those 20% depends on the code, and which on the machine the run happened on and its neighbours?
    options:
      a: "Store the absolute results of every main run and fail the PR build when a benchmark is more than 5% slower than the last stored value"
      b: "Run the baseline (main) and the candidate (PR) in the same CI job on the same dedicated machine and compare them with a statistical test using a threshold above the measured noise"
      c: "Keep the shared runners but raise the BenchmarkDotNet iteration count many times so the error becomes small, and compare the result with the stored values"
      d: "Remove benchmarks from CI: they are useless on shared runners, so find regressions through user complaints and production metrics"
    optionExplanations:
      a: "The stored value was measured on a different machine in a different environment, so the difference from it mostly reflects noise, not code. A 5% threshold with 20% spread guarantees constant false alarms, and a real 10% regression cannot be told apart from random luck."
      c: "More iterations narrow the confidence interval within one run on one machine, but the difference between machines (CPU model, frequency, turbo, neighbours on the virtual machine) is systematic and does not average out. Narrow intervals only create false confidence when compared with numbers from other hardware."
      d: "This gives up early detection: the regression is found weeks later, when nobody knows which commit introduced it, and fixing it costs more. The problem is the comparison method, not the idea of checking performance in CI."
    answer: "Run the baseline and the candidate in the same CI job on the same dedicated machine and compare them with a statistical test using a threshold above the measured noise."
    explanation: |
      A benchmark result is a property of the pair "code plus environment". On shared runners the environment differs
      every time: different hardware, different neighbours on the host, different cache and CPU frequency state. That is
      why absolute numbers from different runs cannot be compared: a 20% spread hides almost any regression worth catching.
      The BenchmarkDotNet good practices also come down to comparing results in the same controlled environment and
      removing background load.

      A scheme that works:

      - **One environment for both versions.** In one job, build main and the PR branch and run the benchmarks of both on
        the same machine, interleaved if possible. Environment noise then affects both versions roughly equally, and the
        difference mostly reflects the code.
      - **A dedicated machine.** A separate self-hosted runner or a physical machine with no neighbours and fixed power
        settings sharply reduces the spread between runs.
      - **Statistics instead of a single number.** Compare the distributions of measurements with a statistical test (for
        example Mann-Whitney, which BenchmarkDotNet can compute) and a threshold chosen above the measured noise. The
        threshold is tuned with "same code against same code" runs.

      For a lead the process side matters too: a flaky check is worse than none, because it teaches the team to ignore red
      builds. So start with a small set of critical benchmarks, agree who triages the alerts, and make the check blocking
      only after the false alarm rate is acceptable. Allocation metrics (`[MemoryDiagnoser]`) are usually far more stable
      than time and complement such a check well.
    linkTitles:
      - BenchmarkDotNet good practices
      - Statistical testing in BenchmarkDotNet

    title: You are given a task with a deadline in a technology you have never used. How do you handle it?

      You write C#, but you are assigned a task with a firm deadline in an unfamiliar technology: for example,
      extending a data pipeline written in Python, which you have never worked with. How do you approach the

    answer: |
      1. **Name the gap as soon as you take the task.** Say that the technology is new to you and put learning
         time into the estimate and the plan. If the deadline cannot fit that time, discuss the options with
         whoever assigns the work: move the date, cut the scope, pair you with an experienced colleague or give
         the task to them. The decision should be a conscious one, not a surprise on the last day.
      2. **Timebox the learning.** Not "learn Python", but the minimum the task needs: run the pipeline locally,
         run the tests, make a trivial change and take it all the way to an environment. For example one or two
         days; if there is no progress by then, that is a signal to report.
      3. **Lean on the existing code.** How this repository handles dependencies, tests, linters and style.
         New code should look like this team's code, not like C# rewritten in Python.
      4. **Bring in someone experienced.** A short pairing session at the start, a discussion of the approach
         before the main implementation, and the usual code review. Batch your questions, but do not sit stuck
         for half a day.
      5. **Work in small steps and show work early.** A first small pull request as soon as possible, so that a
         wrong approach is found while it is still cheap to fix.
      6. **Be open about progress and risks.** At the daily, and if the deadline is at risk, right away, not on
         the due date.
      7. **Leave the knowledge with the team.** Notes on running the code and its pitfalls, an updated README.

      unfamiliar; copy ready-made solutions from the internet or an AI assistant without understanding them;
      rewrite the component in C# without agreement because that feels more comfortable.
    explanation: |
      The question does not test knowledge of Python but honesty, the ability to plan your own learning and to
      ask for help in time. An estimate with no learning time in it is wrong from the start, and a hidden gap
      usually turns into a missed deadline at the point where nothing can be fixed any more.

      The Scrum Guide puts this on the person doing the work: the Developers who will do the work are
      responsible for sizing backlog items, and the Developers create the plan for the Sprint. So the person
      who knows about the gap is the one who has to account for it in the estimate. The Daily Scrum exists to
      inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan in time, and one of the Scrum values is
      openness: the team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges.

      The article on pair programming on Martin Fowler's site names knowledge sharing and onboarding among the
      main benefits of pairing. For knowledge transfer it recommends strong-style pairing: the novice is at the
      keyboard and the experienced colleague navigates, so every idea goes through the hands of the person who
      is learning. An hour of this at the start often saves days of searching alone.
    linkTitles:
      - "On Pair Programming (martinfowler.com)"
      - "The Scrum Guide"

  en:
    title: "A teammate admits their change corrupted customer records and asks you to tell no one while they fix it. What do you do?"
    prompt: |
      A teammate tells you in confidence that their change, released last week, quietly corrupted some customer
      records (for example, it recalculated account balances incorrectly). They are already writing a fix and ask
      you not to tell anyone: they are worried about their reputation. According to them, nobody has noticed yet.

      What do you do?
    hint: "Who besides the two of you is affected, and what are those people doing with the corrupted data right now?"
    answer: |
      1. **Do not promise silence.** Listen without reproach, but say honestly right away that you cannot keep it
         secret: customers are affected.
      2. **Find out the scope and stop the damage.** Is the change still corrupting data, how many records are
         affected, since when. If the corruption is ongoing, stop it first: roll the change back or turn off the
         feature flag.
      3. **Explain why a quiet fix is dangerous.** Customers and support are making decisions on wrong data right
         now. Backups with correct data may age out of their retention period. A fix script without review and
         testing may corrupt even more. If the problem surfaces later, it will look like a cover-up rather than a
         mistake.
      4. **Push them to report it themselves, now.** To the team lead or through the incident process, today. Offer
         help: go together, help assess the scope, draft a short description.
      5. **Set a clear boundary.** If they do not report it within a short agreed time (for example, by the end of
         the day), you will report it yourself. Tell them this up front instead of acting behind their back.
      6. **Keep the review about the process, not the person.** Propose a blameless postmortem: why the change got
         through unnoticed (no test, review, data validation or monitoring). How and when to notify customers is
         decided by management and, if needed, legal, especially if personal data is involved.
    explanation: |
      This is loyalty to a colleague against responsibility to users. A promise of silence protects one person,
      while the harm from corrupted data falls on customers who do not know about it and cannot protect
      themselves. Principle 1.2 of the ACM Code of Ethics ("Avoid harm") requires those who caused unintended harm
      to undo or mitigate it as much as possible, and that cannot be done secretly and alone. Principle 1.7 on
      confidentiality also does not oblige you to keep secret what is evidence of a violation of law,
      organisational regulations or the Code itself.

      The Google SRE book explains why a blame culture is dangerous: people start sweeping incidents and issues
      under the rug, and the risk to the organisation grows. The teammate's request is a typical symptom of that
      fear. So a strong answer does not turn the situation into informing on someone: you give the teammate the
      chance to own it, you help them, and you move the conversation to the systemic causes that let the bug reach
      customer data.

      Weak answers: agree to stay quiet and wait for the fix; go to the manager behind their back at once without
      giving them a chance to report it; blame the teammate publicly. The short deadline matters: every day of
      silence increases the damage and lowers the chance of recovering the data.
    linkTitles:
      - "Site Reliability Engineering, Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure"
      - "ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct"

    title: Тимлид внезапно ушёл, и от вас неформально ждут, что вы его замените. Что вы сделаете?

      отдела и команда уже ждут, что вы проведёте планирование спринта, будете общаться с заинтересованными

      Что вы будете делать и в каком порядке?
    hint: Какие вопросы о вашей новой роли пока никто не задал вслух и кто может на них ответить?
    answer: |
      1. **Не отказываться и не брать всё молча.** Временно подхватить срочное, чтобы ничего не упало:
         ближайшее планирование, обещания заинтересованным сторонам, открытые инциденты и согласования.
         Параллельно составить список того, что делал ушедший тимлид: встречи, решения, доступы, найм,
         разговоры один на один, дежурства.
      2. **В первые дни явно договориться с руководителем.** Прийти к тому, кому подчинялся тимлид, со
         списком и обсудить:
         - **объём**: какие обязанности вы берёте (планирование, общение с заказчиками), а какие остаются у
           руководителя (оценка сотрудников, зарплаты, найм);
         - **полномочия**: можете ли вы обещать сроки, менять приоритеты, одобрять релизы, решать конфликты;
         - **срок**: до найма нового тимлида или до конкретной даты, когда договорённость пересматривается;
         - **что снимается с вас**: какие ваши задачи передаются другим или переносятся и насколько
           уменьшается ваша нагрузка как разработчика;
         - **признание**: как роль оформляется и учитывается в оценке, считается ли она шагом к позиции тимлида.

         Итог зафиксировать письменно, хотя бы коротким письмом.
      3. **Перестроить свою работу.** Отдать задачи на критическом пути другим разработчикам, себе оставить

      4. **Объявить договорённость.** Руководитель сообщает команде и заинтересованным сторонам, за что вы

    explanation: |
      Самый частый сценарий провала - молча взять на себя обе роли. Тогда ни одна не выполняется хорошо:
      время уходит на планирование и встречи, ваши задачи сдвигаются, но никто об этом не знает, потому что

      обязательны ли ваши решения, а заказчики получают обещания, которые вы не вправе давать. Когда что-то
      срывается, непонятно, кто за это отвечал, и виноватым обычно оказывается тот, кто тащил всё на себе.

      результат включает и ответственность за то, чтобы договорённость была выполнимой: явно назвать, что вы

    linkTitles:

      - "Принципы лидерства Amazon"
  en:
    title: Your team lead left suddenly and you are informally expected to fill in. What do you do?
    prompt: |
      Your team lead quit unexpectedly and no replacement has been found yet. Nothing was announced
      officially, but the department head and the team already expect you to run sprint planning, deal with
      the stakeholders and answer their questions about dates. Meanwhile nobody has taken any of your own
      tasks off you, and some of them are on the critical path of the release.

      What do you do, and in what order?
    hint: Which questions about your new role has nobody asked out loud yet, and who can answer them?
    answer: |
      1. **Neither refuse nor silently take everything on.** Temporarily pick up what is urgent so nothing
         drops: the next planning session, promises made to stakeholders, open incidents and approvals. In
         parallel, list what the departed lead used to do: meetings, decisions, access rights, hiring,
         one-on-ones, on-call duties.
      2. **Within the first days, agree on it explicitly with management.** Go to the lead's manager with
         the list and discuss:
         - **scope**: which duties you take on (planning, talking to stakeholders) and which stay with the
           manager (performance reviews, salaries, hiring);
         - **authority**: whether you may commit to dates, change priorities, approve releases, settle
           conflicts;
         - **duration**: until a new lead is hired, or until a specific date when the arrangement is reviewed;
         - **what is taken off you**: which of your tasks move to others or are postponed, and how much your
           load as a developer goes down;
         - **recognition**: how the role is formalised and counted in your review, and whether it is a step
           towards the lead position.

         Write down the outcome, at least as a short email.
      3. **Rearrange your own work.** Hand your critical-path tasks to other developers and keep the ones
         whose delay does not block the team. Otherwise you become the bottleneck in both roles at once.
      4. **Announce the arrangement.** The manager tells the team and the stakeholders what you are
         temporarily responsible for, with what authority and until when. Without that, your decisions are
         taken as personal opinion.
      5. **Distribute instead of centralising.** Planning is the whole team's work, backlog priorities are the
         product owner's area, and the Scrum Master helps remove impediments, if those roles exist. Delegate
         parts of the work to colleagues who want to grow.
      6. **Check in regularly.** Every one or two weeks go over with the manager what works, what is slipping
         and whether you need help. Report overload early and with facts (which tasks have slipped), not when
         something has already failed.
      7. **Finish cleanly.** When a new lead arrives, hand over: decisions, agreements, open risks. If the role
         interests you, say openly that you want to apply for it.
    explanation: |
      The most common way to fail is to silently absorb both roles. Then neither is done well: time goes into
      planning and meetings, your tasks slip, but nobody knows, because formally your load has not changed.
      Unclear authority adds conflict: the team does not know whether your decisions are binding, and
      stakeholders get promises you have no right to make. When something fails, it is unclear who was
      responsible, and the blame usually lands on the person who was carrying everything.

      Refusing with "that's not my job" is a weak answer too. Amazon's Ownership leadership principle
      describes owners as people who never say "that's not my job". But owning the outcome includes owning
      whether the arrangement is workable: stating explicitly what you do, with what authority and at the
      expense of what.

      The 2020 Scrum Guide does not describe a team lead role at all: a Scrum Team has a Product Owner, a
      Scrum Master and Developers, and it is self-managing, deciding internally who does what, when and how.
      The Product Owner is accountable for Product Backlog management, and the Developers create the plan for
      the Sprint. If the team works in Scrum or close to it, this is a good argument not to take over
      everything the lead did, but to hand part of the duties back to those who already own them. At senior
      level the interviewer looks for exactly this: willingness to pick up the work, and the skill to make the
      arrangement explicit and sustainable.
    linkTitles:
      - "The Scrum Guide"
      - "Amazon leadership principles"

  ru:
    title: Что делают Pod, Deployment и Service, когда .NET API работает в Kubernetes?
    prompt: |
      API на ASP.NET Core упаковано в контейнерный образ и развёрнуто в Kubernetes в трёх репликах. В манифестах
      описаны объекты `Deployment` и `Service`, а `kubectl get pods` показывает три работающих Pod.

      За что отвечает каждый из этих объектов - Pod, Deployment и Service? Почему клиенты обращаются к сервису,
      а не напрямую к IP-адресам Pod?
    hint: Что происходит с Pod и его IP-адресом, когда контейнер падает или выкатывается другая версия образа?

        с API), которые запускаются на одном узле, делят сетевое пространство (один IP-адрес и набор портов) и
        могут делить тома. Pod эфемерен: упавший Pod не чинят, а заменяют другим, и у замены другой IP-адрес.
        Поэтому Pod обычно не создают вручную.
      - **Deployment** - контроллер, которому описывают желаемое состояние: шаблон Pod (образ, переменные
        окружения, порты, проверки) и число реплик. Через ReplicaSet он поддерживает это число: если Pod или
        узел пропал, создаётся замена. При изменении шаблона, например тега образа, Deployment выкатывает версию
        постепенно (стратегия по умолчанию - `RollingUpdate`) и позволяет откатиться на предыдущую ревизию.
      - **Service** - стабильное DNS-имя в кластере и виртуальный IP-адрес перед группой Pod, которую он
        выбирает по меткам (`selector`). Запросы на порт сервиса распределяются между подходящими готовыми Pod
        и направляются на `targetPort` контейнера. Клиентам не нужно знать IP-адреса Pod, которые меняются
        при каждом перезапуске и выкатке.
    explanation: |
      Три объекта разделяют три вопроса. Pod отвечает на вопрос «что и как запустить», Deployment - «сколько
      копий и какой версии должно работать», Service - «как до них достучаться». Kubernetes постоянно приводит
      кластер к описанному состоянию, поэтому отдельные Pod появляются и исчезают, а адрес сервиса остаётся
      прежним.

      Типичные ошибки:

      - Pod создан напрямую, без Deployment: после сбоя или потери узла его никто не пересоздаст.
      - Метки в `selector` сервиса не совпадают с метками шаблона Pod: у сервиса нет конечных точек, и запросы
        никуда не доходят.

        с .NET 8 это порт 8080, а не 80.

      Тип сервиса по умолчанию - `ClusterIP`: он доступен только внутри кластера. Чтобы открыть API наружу,

      - "Kubernetes: Deployments"
      - "Kubernetes: Service"
  en:
    title: What do a Pod, a Deployment and a Service do when a .NET API runs in Kubernetes?
    prompt: |
      An ASP.NET Core API is packaged as a container image and deployed to Kubernetes with three replicas. The
      manifests describe a `Deployment` and a `Service` object, and `kubectl get pods` shows three running Pods.

      What is each of these objects - Pod, Deployment and Service - responsible for? Why do clients call the
      Service instead of the IP addresses of the Pods?
    hint: What happens to a Pod and its IP address when the container crashes or another version of the image is rolled out?
    answer: |
      - **Pod** is the smallest deployable unit. It is one or more containers (usually one container with the
        API) that run on the same node, share a network namespace (one IP address and one set of ports) and can
        share volumes. A Pod is ephemeral: a failed Pod is not repaired but replaced by another one, and the
        replacement has a different IP address. That is why Pods are usually not created by hand.
      - **Deployment** is a controller that you give a desired state: a Pod template (image, environment
        variables, ports, probes) and a number of replicas. Through a ReplicaSet it keeps that number: if a Pod
        or a node disappears, a replacement is created. When the template changes, for example the image tag, the
        Deployment rolls the version out gradually (the default strategy is `RollingUpdate`) and lets you roll
        back to the previous revision.
      - **Service** is a stable DNS name inside the cluster and a virtual IP address in front of a group of Pods
        that it selects by labels (`selector`). Requests to the Service port are spread across the matching ready
        Pods and sent to the container `targetPort`. Clients do not need the IP addresses of the Pods, which change
        on every restart and rollout.
    explanation: |
      The three objects split three concerns. The Pod answers "what to run and how", the Deployment answers "how
      many copies of which version must run", and the Service answers "how to reach them". Kubernetes keeps
      driving the cluster towards the described state, so individual Pods come and go while the Service address
      stays the same.

      Common mistakes:

      - A Pod is created directly, without a Deployment: after a crash or a lost node nobody recreates it.
      - The labels in the Service `selector` do not match the labels of the Pod template: the Service has no
        endpoints and requests go nowhere.
      - `targetPort` does not match the port Kestrel listens on. In the official ASP.NET Core images starting
        with .NET 8 that port is 8080, not 80.

      The default Service type is `ClusterIP`: it is reachable only inside the cluster. To expose the API
      outside, use a Service of type `LoadBalancer`, or Ingress and the Gateway API on top of a regular Service.
    linkTitles:
      - "Kubernetes: Pods"
      - "Kubernetes: Deployments"
      - "Kubernetes: Service"

    explanation: |
      Base64 - это кодирование, а не шифрование: оно нужно, чтобы в YAML и JSON можно было хранить произвольные
      байты, и обращается командой `base64 -d` без всякого ключа. По умолчанию Kubernetes хранит Secret в etcd

  en:
    title: How is the value of a Kubernetes Secret protected by default?
    prompt: |
      A team stores the database connection string of a .NET service in a `Secret` object and passes it to the
      container through an environment variable. The cluster administrator has configured nothing for data
      encryption.

      How is the value of this Secret protected by default?
    hint: How does encoding differ from encryption, and where does the API server store cluster objects?
    options:
      a: "The API server encrypts the value with a cluster key, and etcd stores only the ciphertext."
      b: "The value is only base64-encoded and stored unencrypted in etcd: anyone who may read this Secret through the API, or who has access to etcd, can read it."
      c: "etcd stores only a hash of the value, so the original string cannot be recovered from storage."
      d: "Only the Pods that reference the Secret see the value, and API users are shown a masked value."
    optionExplanations:
      a: "Without encryption at rest configured (`--encryption-provider-config` on `kube-apiserver`), the API server writes the Secret to etcd as is, unencrypted."
      c: "A hash is irreversible, and the container needs the original connection string. Kubernetes stores the value itself, base64-encoded, and gives it to the Pod in full."
      d: "There is no masking: `kubectl get secret -o yaml` returns the `data` field in base64, which decodes without any key. Also, anyone who can create a Pod in the namespace can mount any Secret of that namespace into it and read the value."
    answer: "The value is only base64-encoded and stored unencrypted in etcd: anyone who may read this Secret through the API, or who has access to etcd, can read it."
    explanation: |
      Base64 is an encoding, not encryption: it exists so that YAML and JSON can carry arbitrary bytes, and
      `base64 -d` reverses it without any key. By default Kubernetes stores Secrets in etcd unencrypted. So the
      value is available to anyone with `get` or `list` rights on Secrets in that namespace, to anyone who can
      create a Pod there (including indirectly, through a Deployment), and to anyone who gets access to etcd or
      its backups.

      Protection comes from several measures:

      - **Encryption at rest.** The API server is started with `--encryption-provider-config` pointing at an
        `EncryptionConfiguration` with an encryption provider, preferably `kms` with the key in an external key
        store. Only writes made after enabling it are encrypted, so existing Secrets must be rewritten. In
        managed clusters the defaults depend on the provider; check its documentation.
      - **Least-privilege RBAC.** Encryption protects etcd and backups, not reads through the API: grant rights
        on Secrets and on creating Pods only to those who need them.
      - **No values in Git.** A Secret manifest with base64 data in a repository is equivalent to a plain-text
        password.

      - "Kubernetes: Secrets"
      - "Kubernetes: Encrypting confidential data at rest"

    prompt: |
      API на ASP.NET Core развёрнут в Kubernetes через Deployment. У контейнера настроены три проверки:
      `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` и `startupProbe`.

      Что происходит с контейнером, подом и входящим трафиком, когда не проходит каждая из этих проверок?
      Какие эндпоинты здоровья из этого следует сделать в приложении?
    hint: Какая проверка отвечает на вопрос «можно ли сейчас слать сюда трафик», а какая - «нужно ли перезапустить процесс»?
    answer: |
      - **Readiness.** После `failureThreshold` неудачных проверок подряд kubelet помечает контейнер как неготовый,
        условие пода `Ready` становится `False`, и IP пода убирается из конечных точек всех Service, которые
        выбирают этот под. Контейнер **не перезапускается**: процесс продолжает работать, проверка выполняется всё
        время жизни контейнера, и как только она снова проходит, под возвращается в балансировку. Неготовые поды
        не считаются доступными и при rolling update, поэтому выкатка не продвигается дальше.
      - **Liveness.** После `failureThreshold` неудач подряд kubelet убивает контейнер, и дальше действует
        `restartPolicy` пода (у подов Deployment это `Always`), то есть контейнер перезапускается. Пересоздаётся
        только контейнер, а не под. Растёт счётчик перезапусков, а при повторяющихся падениях задержка между
        перезапусками увеличивается, и под показывает `CrashLoopBackOff`.
      - **Startup.** Пока startup-проверка не прошла, kubelet не запускает liveness- и readiness-проверки. После
        первого успеха она больше не выполняется, и работу продолжают две другие. Если она не прошла за отведённое
        окно (примерно `failureThreshold * periodSeconds`), kubelet убивает контейнер так же, как при неудачной
        liveness-проверке.

      Для приложения .NET из этого следуют разные эндпоинты: liveness проверяет только то, что сам процесс
      отвечает, а readiness - что сервис может обслуживать запросы прямо сейчас (например, прогрет кэш и доступны
      зависимости). В ASP.NET Core это делают двумя вызовами `MapHealthChecks` с разными наборами проверок,
      отобранными через теги и `HealthCheckOptions.Predicate`.
    explanation: |
      Три проверки отвечают на разные вопросы, поэтому и реакция на их неудачу разная. Readiness описывает
      временное состояние: под может перестать принимать трафик и вернуться без всякого вмешательства, поэтому
      Kubernetes только меняет маршрутизацию. Liveness говорит, что процесс завис и сам не восстановится,
      поэтому единственное действие - перезапуск контейнера. Startup-проверка нужна медленно стартующим
      приложениям: она даёт отдельное, длинное окно на запуск, не заставляя увеличивать задержку и порог
      liveness-проверки, которая потом должна быстро замечать зависание.

      Типичные ошибки: одна и та же проверка для liveness и readiness, из-за которой кратковременная проблема
      с зависимостью превращается в перезапуски всех подов; слишком строгая liveness-проверка без startup-проверки,
      из-за которой контейнер убивают раньше, чем приложение успевает стартовать, и он уходит в цикл перезапусков.
      Если readiness-проверка не настроена, Kubernetes считает контейнер готовым сразу после запуска процесса,
      и трафик может прийти до того, как Kestrel начнёт принимать соединения.

      - "Настройка liveness-, readiness- и startup-проверок (документация Kubernetes)"
      - "Жизненный цикл пода (документация Kubernetes)"
  en:
    title: What does Kubernetes do when a liveness, readiness or startup probe of a container fails?
    prompt: |
      An ASP.NET Core API runs in Kubernetes through a Deployment. Its container has three probes configured:
      `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` and `startupProbe`.

      What happens to the container, the Pod and incoming traffic when each of these probes fails? Which health
      endpoints should the app expose as a result?
    hint: Which probe answers "may traffic be sent here right now", and which answers "should the process be restarted"?
    answer: |
      - **Readiness.** After `failureThreshold` consecutive failures the kubelet marks the container as not ready,
        the Pod's `Ready` condition becomes `False`, and the Pod IP is removed from the endpoints of every Service
        that selects the Pod. The container is **not restarted**: the process keeps running, the probe keeps
        running for the whole life of the container, and once it passes again the Pod is put back into load
        balancing. Pods that are not ready are not counted as available during a rolling update either, so the
        rollout does not progress.
      - **Liveness.** After `failureThreshold` consecutive failures the kubelet kills the container, and the
        Pod's `restartPolicy` applies (for Deployment Pods it is `Always`), so the container is restarted. Only the
        container is recreated, not the Pod. The restart count grows, and with repeated failures the delay between
        restarts increases and the Pod shows `CrashLoopBackOff`.
      - **Startup.** Until the startup probe succeeds, the kubelet does not run the liveness and readiness probes.
        After its first success it is not run again, and the other two take over. If it does not succeed within
        its window (roughly `failureThreshold * periodSeconds`), the kubelet kills the container just as it does
        after a failed liveness probe.

      For a .NET app this means separate endpoints: liveness checks only that the process itself responds, and
      readiness checks that the service can handle requests right now (for example, the cache is warm and
      dependencies are reachable). In ASP.NET Core this is done with two `MapHealthChecks` calls that run different
      sets of checks, selected by tags and `HealthCheckOptions.Predicate`.
    explanation: |
      The three probes answer different questions, so the reaction to their failure differs. Readiness describes
      a temporary state: a Pod can stop taking traffic and come back without any intervention, so Kubernetes
      only changes routing. Liveness says that the process is stuck and will not recover by itself, so the only
      action is to restart the container. The startup probe exists for slow-starting apps: it gives a separate,
      long window for startup without forcing a long delay and threshold on the liveness probe, which should
      later detect a hang quickly.

      Typical mistakes: one probe used for both liveness and readiness, which turns a short dependency problem
      into restarts of every Pod; a strict liveness probe without a startup probe, which kills the container
      before the app finishes starting and sends it into a restart loop. If no readiness probe is configured,
      Kubernetes treats the container as ready as soon as the process starts, and traffic can arrive before
      Kestrel accepts connections.
    linkTitles:
      - "Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes (Kubernetes docs)"
      - "Pod Lifecycle (Kubernetes docs)"

      которые выполняются до публикации на машине сборки, например сборку фронтенда, можно встроить в MSBuild, и для
      них Dockerfile не нужен.

      Важная деталь: образы .NET 8 и более поздних версий по умолчанию запускают приложение от непривилегированного
      пользователя `app`, и SDK сохраняет это поведение. В .NET 7 эта возможность поставлялась отдельным пакетом
      `Microsoft.NET.Build.Containers`, а начиная с .NET 8 SDK встроена в SDK. Сказанное верно и для .NET 10 SDK.

  en:
    title: What does dotnet publish with the PublishContainer target do, and when do you still need a Dockerfile?
    prompt: |
      Starting with the .NET 8 SDK you can build a container image of an app without a Dockerfile, for example with
      `dotnet publish --os linux --arch x64 -t:PublishContainer`.

      What exactly does this command do, how does the SDK choose the base image, and when do you still need a Dockerfile?
    hint: Which Dockerfile instructions come down to image metadata and copying files, and which ones need a command to run inside the image being built?
    answer: |
      - **What it does.** The SDK publishes the app like a normal `dotnet publish`, then builds an OCI image itself:
        it takes the base image from a registry, adds a layer with the publish output on top and writes the image
        configuration (entry point, working directory, user, ports, environment variables). Neither a Dockerfile nor
        `docker build` is involved.
      - **Where it goes.** By default the image is loaded into the local Docker (or Podman) daemon, and only that step
        needs a container engine. With the `ContainerRegistry` property the SDK pushes the image straight to a
        registry, and with `ContainerArchiveOutputPath` it writes a `.tar.gz` archive.
      - **Base image.** The SDK infers it from the project type: `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet` for ASP.NET Core,
        `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/runtime` for a console app, `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/runtime-deps` for a
        self-contained app and Native AOT. The tag matches the target framework version of the project. You override
        the choice with `ContainerBaseImage` (any image) and `ContainerFamily` (a variant of the same image, such as
        `alpine` or chiseled).
      - **Configuration.** Name, tags, ports, environment variables and user are MSBuild properties and items:
        `ContainerRepository`, `ContainerImageTags`, `ContainerPort`, `ContainerEnvironmentVariable`, `ContainerUser`.
      - **When you need a Dockerfile.** The SDK has no equivalent of the `RUN` instruction: it does not run commands
        inside the image. If you need extra OS packages (fonts, `libgdiplus`, client tools), directories or files in
        the image outside the publish output, a script that runs during the image build, or several apps in one image,
        you need a Dockerfile. A common compromise is to build your own base image with the needed packages from a
        Dockerfile, set it as `ContainerBaseImage`, and keep publishing the app through the SDK.
    explanation: |
      A container image is a set of file system layers plus a JSON configuration. For a typical .NET app a Dockerfile
      does little: it takes the official runtime image, copies the `dotnet publish` output and sets `ENTRYPOINT`,
      `WORKDIR`, `USER` and `EXPOSE`. The SDK can do all of that on its own: it packs the publish output as a layer
      archive and writes the configuration from project properties. Building the image becomes part of MSBuild and needs
      no container engine until the image has to be loaded into the local Docker.

      The line is drawn at `RUN`. To run `apt-get install` or any script, a build engine such as BuildKit has to start a
      container from an intermediate image and commit the changes to its file system. The SDK does not do that, so
      anything that needs commands inside the image stays with a Dockerfile. Steps that run on the build machine before
      publishing, such as a front-end build, can be wired into MSBuild and need no Dockerfile.

      One detail: .NET 8 and later images run the app as the non-root `app` user by default, and the SDK keeps that
      behaviour. In .NET 7 the feature shipped as the separate `Microsoft.NET.Build.Containers` package; starting with
      the .NET 8 SDK it is built into the SDK. All of this also holds for the .NET 10 SDK.
    linkTitles:
      - "Containerize a .NET app with dotnet publish"
      - ".NET container images"

    title: Какая строка Dockerfile оставляет токен приватного фида NuGet в опубликованном образе?

      Этот образ запускает интеграционные тесты в CI, поэтому он намеренно построен на образе SDK. Его публикуют во
      внутренний реестр, откуда его забирают другие команды. Пакеты восстанавливаются из приватного фида NuGet:

      `ClearTextPassword="%NUGET_TOKEN%"`. CI собирает образ командой
      `docker build --build-arg NUGET_TOKEN=<token> .`.

      Сканер безопасности реестра нашёл действующий токен фида в опубликованном образе. Щёлкните по строке, из-за
      которой токен попал в образ.
    hint: Какие сведения, кроме файловых слоёв, хранятся в образе и видны через `docker inspect` и `docker history`?
    answer: Строка 3, `ENV NUGET_TOKEN=$NUGET_TOKEN`, вместе с передачей токена через `ARG` в строке 2.
    explanation: |
      Инструкция `ENV` записывает переменную в конфигурацию образа. Значение токена уходит в реестр вместе с образом:
      его показывает `docker inspect` в `Config.Env`, и оно есть в окружении каждого контейнера, запущенного из образа.

      ссылается, теперь живёт в образе навсегда.

      Передача через `ARG` без `ENV` тоже не решает проблему. Значения аргументов сборки, которые используют
      инструкции `RUN`, сохраняются в истории образа, и документация Docker прямо предупреждает, что аргументы сборки
      видны в `docker history` и в provenance-аттестациях. Поэтому принимаются и строка 3, и строка 2: обе - способ

      Исправление - убрать строки 2 и 3 и передать токен как секрет BuildKit только в тот шаг, которому он нужен:
      `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=nuget_token,env=NUGET_TOKEN dotnet restore IntegrationTests/IntegrationTests.csproj`,

      этого `RUN` и не попадает ни в слои, ни в историю, ни в кэш сборки. Последующим `dotnet build --no-restore` и

      тега из реестра не удаляет копии. В многоэтапной сборке `ENV` этапа сборки не наследуется последним этапом, но
      токен всё равно остаётся в метаданных и кэше этапа сборки, поэтому и там правильный инструмент - монтирование
      секрета.

  en:
    title: Which Dockerfile line leaves the private NuGet feed token in the published image?
    prompt: |
      This image runs integration tests in CI, so it is based on the SDK image on purpose. It is pushed to an internal
      registry, where other teams pull it. Packages are restored from a private NuGet feed: the `nuget.config` in the
      repository does not hold the token itself but refers to an environment variable,
      `ClearTextPassword="%NUGET_TOKEN%"`. CI builds the image with
      `docker build --build-arg NUGET_TOKEN=<token> .`.

      The registry security scanner found a valid feed token in the published image. Click the line that put the
      token into the image.
    hint: What information, apart from the file system layers, is stored in an image and shown by `docker inspect` and `docker history`?
    answer: Line 3, `ENV NUGET_TOKEN=$NUGET_TOKEN`, together with passing the token through `ARG` on line 2.
    explanation: |
      The `ENV` instruction writes the variable into the image configuration. The token value travels to the registry
      with the image: `docker inspect` shows it in `Config.Env`, and it is in the environment of every container started
      from the image. The `nuget.config` itself is safe because it holds only the `%NUGET_TOKEN%` reference, but the
      variable it refers to now lives in the image for good.

      Passing it through `ARG` without `ENV` does not solve the problem either. The values of build arguments used by
      `RUN` instructions are kept in the image history, and the Docker documentation warns that build arguments are
      visible in `docker history` and in provenance attestations. That is why both line 3 and line 2 are accepted: each
      is a way of passing a secret that was not designed for secrets.

      The fix is to remove lines 2 and 3 and pass the token as a BuildKit secret only to the step that needs it:
      `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=nuget_token,env=NUGET_TOKEN dotnet restore IntegrationTests/IntegrationTests.csproj`,
      built with `docker build --secret id=nuget_token,env=NUGET_TOKEN .`. The secret is available only during that
      `RUN` and ends up in no layer, no history entry and no build cache. The later `dotnet build --no-restore` and
      `dotnet test --no-build` no longer need the feed.

      The token that has already leaked must be revoked and replaced: anyone who pulled the image can read it, and
      deleting the tag from the registry does not delete the copies. In a multi-stage build the last stage does not
      inherit the `ENV` of the build stage, but the token still stays in the metadata and cache of the build stage, so
      a secret mount is the right tool there as well.
    linkTitles:
      - "Docker build secrets"
      - "Dockerfile reference"

    title: Какая строка манифеста не даёт приложению увидеть изменения ConfigMap?

      Сервис на ASP.NET Core в .NET 10 создаётся через `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`, который подключает
      `appsettings.json` с `reloadOnChange: true`, а настройки читаются через `IOptionsMonitor<T>`. Файл
      `appsettings.json` приходит в контейнер из ConfigMap `orders-api-config`.

      После `kubectl apply` с изменённым ConfigMap прошло полчаса, но в контейнере по-прежнему лежит старый файл,
      и приложение работает со старыми значениями. Помогает только перезапуск Pod. Щёлкните по строке манифеста,
      из-за которой обновление не доходит до контейнера.
    hint: Как kubelet доставляет новое содержимое ConfigMap в уже смонтированный том, и работает ли это для любого способа монтирования?

      символическая ссылка `..data`, а видимые файлы - это ссылки через `..data`. При изменении ConfigMap kubelet
      записывает новый каталог и атомарно переключает `..data`. Изменение приходит не мгновенно, а с задержкой
      порядка периода синхронизации kubelet плюс время жизни его кэша.

    hint: How does the kubelet deliver new ConfigMap content into a volume that is already mounted, and does that work for every way of mounting it?
    answer: Line 21, `subPath: appsettings.json` in the volume mount.
    explanation: |
      When a ConfigMap is mounted as a whole volume, the kubelet keeps the files in a hidden directory that the
      symbolic link `..data` points to, and the visible files are links through `..data`. When the ConfigMap
      changes, the kubelet writes a new directory and atomically switches `..data`. The change is not instant: it
      arrives after about the kubelet sync period plus the lifetime of its cache.

      With `subPath` the mechanism is different: a specific file is mounted into the container as it was when the
      container started. The Kubernetes documentation states directly that a container using a ConfigMap as a
      `subPath` volume mount does not receive ConfigMap updates. The file inside the container never changes, so
      `reloadOnChange` and `IOptionsMonitor<T>` are not to blame: the file watcher has nothing to notice. Line 20
      is not a defect on its own, it only sets the path for this single-file mount.

      The `subPath` is there for a reason: mounting the whole volume at `/app` would hide the published app
      files. The proper fix is to mount the whole ConfigMap into a separate directory, for example `/app/config`,
      and add the file explicitly:
      `builder.Configuration.AddJsonFile("/app/config/appsettings.json", optional: true, reloadOnChange: true)`.
      The source added last overrides values from the sources added before it. If the file watcher does not
      notice the symbolic link switch, polling can be turned on with the environment variable
      `DOTNET_USE_POLLING_FILE_WATCHER=true`.

      Values passed from a ConfigMap through environment variables are not updated without a restart either.
      That is why many teams do not rely on hot reload at all and ship a configuration change as a new version: a
      checksum of the ConfigMap in a Pod template annotation triggers a rolling update of the Deployment.

      - "ConfigMaps (Kubernetes docs)"
      - "Configuration in ASP.NET Core"
