  en:
    title: A .NET API in Kubernetes with a CPU limit of 1 has p99 spikes at 40% average CPU
    prompt: |
      An ASP.NET Core API (.NET 10) runs in Kubernetes on nodes with 8 cores. The container has `limits.cpu: 1`.
      The dashboard shows average CPU usage around 40% of the limit, but p99 latency regularly jumps several times
      higher while p50 stays normal. There are no errors in the logs and memory is fine.

      What do you check and what do you change, and in what order?
    hint: Are the average usage over a minute and the limit that the kernel enforces in every short interval the same thing? And how many processors does the .NET runtime see?
    answer: |
      1. **Confirm throttling instead of looking at usage.** Compare `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total`
         with `container_cpu_cfs_periods_total` (cAdvisor metrics), or the `nr_throttled` and `throttled_usec`
         fields in the container's `cpu.stat`. A noticeable share of throttled periods that lines up in time with
         the p99 spikes confirms the cause. Average usage over a 15-60 second scrape interval does not show it.
      2. **Check what the runtime sees.** With a limit of 1, `Environment.ProcessorCount` returns 1 in the
         container. Collect counters with `dotnet-counters`: thread pool queue length and thread count, GC pause
         time. A growing thread pool queue with few threads points to thread pool starvation, and long pauses point
         to a garbage collector sized for one processor.
      3. **Change the resources.** Set `requests.cpu` to the real steady usage plus a margin (it drives Pod
         placement and the HPA), and remove the CPU limit or raise it well above the request so that short bursts
         are not stopped. If a limit is mandatory (namespace policy, Guaranteed QoS class), give whole cores, for
         example 2, and check that the thread pool and the garbage collector are consistent with the new processor
         count. Keep the memory limit.
      4. **Remove blocking in the code.** Find sync-over-async and other blocking calls that force the thread pool
         to inject threads. Do not raise `ThreadPool.SetMinThreads` blindly. `DOTNET_PROCESSOR_COUNT` can override
         the processor count, but a value above the quota only makes throttling worse.
      5. **Verify and scale out.** Run a load test before and after: p99 and the share of throttled periods. Cover
         further load growth with horizontal scaling (HPA on utilization relative to requests), not with a tight
         per-Pod limit.
    explanation: |
      Kubernetes passes the CPU limit to the Linux kernel as a CFS quota: in every scheduler period (100 ms by
      default) the container gets at most 100 ms of CPU time per CPU of the limit. The quota is shared by all
      threads at once. If on an 8-core node four app threads run in parallel (request handling, JIT, parallel
      garbage collection), they use up the quota in 25 ms, and the whole container is stopped for the rest of the
      period, another 75 ms. A request that falls into such a period gets those milliseconds added to its latency.
      Average usage stays at 40% because the pauses are short and the metric averages them over tens of seconds.
      Hence the picture: p50 is fine, p99 jumps.

      The other half of the problem is in the runtime itself. In .NET 10 `Environment.ProcessorCount` in a
      container takes the CPU limit into account and rounds it up, so with a limit of 1 the app believes it has
      one processor. The minimum number of thread pool threads and the number of server GC heaps depend on that
      number. With one processor the thread pool reacts more slowly to bursts of blocking work, and the garbage
      collector loses its parallelism.

      CPU requests and limits work differently. A request is a guaranteed share under contention for cores and
      the basis for the scheduler and the HPA. A limit is a hard ceiling that applies even when the node is idle.
      That is why for a latency-sensitive API it is usually right to set honest requests and no tight CPU limit.
      The cost of that choice: the Pod gets the Burstable QoS class and its performance depends on free cores on
      the node, so capacity must be planned by requests rather than by hoping for spare cores.
    linkTitles:
      - "Resource management for Pods and containers (Kubernetes docs)"
      - "Environment.ProcessorCount property"
      - "Runtime configuration options for garbage collection"

      2. **Понять причину.** При удалении пода API-сервер помечает его как завершающийся, и дальше параллельно идут

    title: Why does every rolling update of a .NET service cause a burst of 502 errors at the ingress?
    prompt: |
      An ASP.NET Core service (.NET 10) runs in Kubernetes behind an ingress controller. During every rolling update
      the ingress returns a burst of 502 errors to clients for a few seconds. The app handles SIGTERM correctly: the
      logs show that the host stops gracefully and requests already in progress complete. The Pod spec has no
      `lifecycle` section, and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is left at its default.

      What is going on, and what do you change?
    hint: When a Pod is deleted, who learns about it first - the kubelet that sends the signal, or the components that route traffic to the Pod?
    answer: |
      1. **Confirm the error window.** Correlate the 502 timestamps with the termination of old Pods, not the startup
         of new ones. The ingress controller logs show refused or reset connections to the IPs of Pods that are
         already terminating. If the errors hit new Pods, the cause is different - the readiness probe.
      2. **Understand the cause.** When a Pod is deleted, the API server marks it as terminating, and two independent
         processes start in parallel. The kubelet runs the `preStop` hook (there is none here) and sends SIGTERM to
         the container. The EndpointSlice controller removes the Pod from the ready endpoints of the Service, and only
         then do kube-proxy and the ingress controller, each through its own watch on the API, update their routing.
         The signal usually wins: the host starts stopping, Kestrel stops accepting new connections, and the ingress
         keeps sending requests to the Pod IP for a few more seconds and gets refused. Hence the 502s.
      3. **Delay the shutdown with `preStop`.** Add a hook that waits a few seconds (typically 5-15, based on how fast
         your routing converges) before the kubelet sends SIGTERM. The app keeps serving requests normally during that
         time, and routing catches up and drops the Pod. If the cluster version supports the `sleep` hook action, use
         `lifecycle.preStop.sleep.seconds: 10`; otherwise use `exec` with the command `sleep 10`, but that needs a
         `sleep` executable in the image, and chiseled images have none.
      4. **Recalculate `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.** This period (30 seconds by default) counts from the start of
         Pod termination and includes the time spent in `preStop`; when it expires, the process gets SIGKILL. Since
         .NET 8 the default `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` is also 30 seconds, so with a 10 second delay and the
         default period the kubelet can kill the process while it is still draining requests. The period must be at
         least the `preStop` delay plus `ShutdownTimeout` plus a margin, for example 10 + 30 + 5 = 45 seconds, or
         lower `ShutdownTimeout`.
      5. **Lock it in.** Run a rolling update under synthetic load and check that there are no 5xx errors. Make sure
         new Pods have a readiness probe, so traffic reaches them only once they are ready.
    explanation: |
      Handling SIGTERM correctly solves only half of the problem: it lets the requests the app has already accepted
      finish. It cannot help the requests that routing keeps sending after Kestrel has closed its listening socket.
      Kubernetes does not wait for every kube-proxy and ingress controller to learn about the Pod deletion before it
      sends the signal: endpoint removal and container shutdown run independently and agree only eventually.

      The `preStop` hook is the standard way to buy time: SIGTERM is sent only after the hook has completed. A
      readiness probe that starts failing during shutdown does not remove the race: the Pod is already out of the
      ready endpoints, and the delay is in propagating that change to the routers.

      The second trap is `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`. It is shared by `preStop` and the app shutdown, so adding a
      delay without raising the period easily produces new aborted requests, this time from SIGKILL. In .NET 8 the
      default `ShutdownTimeout` grew from 5 to 30 seconds and now equals the Kubernetes default period; the answer
      describes .NET 10 behaviour.
    linkTitles:
      - "Pod lifecycle (Kubernetes docs)"
      - "Container lifecycle hooks (Kubernetes docs)"
      - ".NET Generic Host"

  en:
    title: How should a .NET queue worker in containers be autoscaled, and why does CPU-based scaling fit it poorly?
    prompt: |
      A .NET service (`BackgroundService`) reads messages from a queue (Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ or Kafka) and for
      every message calls a database and an external HTTP API. The service runs in containers, and autoscaling is
      configured on CPU utilization with a 70% target. At peak hours the queue grows to hundreds of thousands of
      messages, yet the replica count does not change.

      Why does this happen, which metric should such a worker scale on, and what else must the scaling setup cover?
    hint: What is the worker process busy with most of the time while it waits for the database and the external API, and which value directly shows that work is not keeping up?
    answer: |
      - **Why CPU does not work.** The worker spends almost all its time waiting on I/O: the broker, the database,
        HTTP. CPU stays low even while the queue grows, so a CPU rule adds no replicas. Conversely, CPU can rise from
        serialization or garbage collection with no backlog at all. CPU is an indirect sign of load; for a queue
        consumer the direct signal is the amount of waiting work.
      - **Scale on the backlog.** The metric is queue length, consumer group lag in Kafka or the age of the oldest
        message. The tools are event-driven scaling: KEDA (AKS has a KEDA add-on) with a `ScaledObject` and the scaler
        for your broker, or Azure Container Apps scale rules, which are built on the same KEDA scalers. You set a
        target number of messages per replica plus minimum and maximum replicas. KEDA can scale to zero, which a plain
        CPU-based HPA does not do.
      - **Derive the per-replica target from throughput.** If one replica handles N messages per second and the
        queue must drain within T seconds, the per-replica target is about N x T.
      - **Cap the maximum by what dependencies can absorb.** Every replica opens database connections and calls the
        external API, so the replica cap follows from the database connection limit, the API rate limits and, for
        Kafka, the partition count (extra consumers in a group sit idle). Otherwise, when the database degrades, the
        queue grows, the scaler adds replicas, and they finish off the same database.
      - **Scale in safely.** On scale-in the container gets SIGTERM: the worker must honour `stoppingToken`, finish or
        release the current message, and `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` plus the container termination grace period
        must cover the processing time. At-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers. A cooldown period
        prevents the replica count from flapping.
      - **Account for cold start.** Scaling to zero saves resources, but the first message after an idle period waits
        for a container to start; if latency matters, keep the minimum at 1.
    explanation: |
      A scaling metric should measure the thing you want to bound. For a queue worker that is how long work waits:
      how many messages are queued and for how long. CPU utilization tracks this only when processing is CPU-bound.
      A typical .NET worker calls the database and services through `async` code, so no thread is busy while it
      waits, CPU stays low, and the backlog grows without limit.

      KEDA handles this as follows: the scaler polls the broker, KEDA itself moves the workload between zero and one
      replica, and scaling from one replica upward is delegated to an HPA that receives the backlog as an external
      metric. Azure Container Apps builds this in: a scale rule names the event source and the threshold, and the
      platform does the rest.

      Backlog-based scaling amplifies feedback from dependencies: if the database slows down, the backlog grows
      because of it, and adding replicas only adds load to the bottleneck. That is why the replica cap is not a
      formality but protection for the dependencies, and it is chosen from their capacity, not from the budget.
    linkTitles:
      - "Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps"
      - "Simplified application autoscaling with the KEDA add-on in AKS"

    explanation: |
      `PodDisruptionBudget` ограничивает только добровольные нарушения, которые проходят через Eviction API.

    title: Which events does a PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable 2 protect a three-replica service from?
    prompt: |
      An ASP.NET Core API runs in Kubernetes as a Deployment of three replicas. A `PodDisruptionBudget` with
      `minAvailable: 2` and a selector for these Pods has been created.

      Which of these events will the budget prevent from leaving fewer than two available Pods?
    hint: Which API call must a component make to remove a Pod for the API server to check the budget at all?
    options:
      a: "Draining a node with `kubectl drain` during a node pool upgrade"
      b: "A node failure: the virtual machine disappears because of a hardware fault"
      c: "The kernel killing the .NET process (OOM kill) when it exceeds the container memory limit"
      d: "A rolling update of the Deployment itself to a new image"
      e: "Deleting Pods with `kubectl delete pod`"
    optionExplanations:
      b: "A node failure is an involuntary disruption: the Pod disappears without any API call, so there is nothing to refuse. The budget does not prevent it, although the lost Pod counts against later evictions."
      c: "An OOM kill is done by the kernel, after which the kubelet restarts the container. The Eviction API is not involved, so the budget is not checked."

    answer: "Draining a node with `kubectl drain` during a node pool upgrade."
    explanation: |
      A `PodDisruptionBudget` limits only voluntary disruptions that go through the Eviction API. Before an eviction
      the API server checks that at least `minAvailable` Pods matching the budget will remain. If not, the request is
      rejected with status 429 and `kubectl drain` retries later. Node drains, cluster autoscaler scale-down and node
      upgrades in managed clusters all work through eviction. With three replicas and `minAvailable: 2`, a drain
      evicts Pods one at a time and waits for the replacement to become ready.

      Involuntary disruptions (a node failure, an OOM kill, a process crash) do not go through the API, so the budget
      cannot stop them. It only counts them: if one Pod is already unavailable because of a failure, the next eviction
      is rejected. Deleting Pods or the Deployment directly and a rolling update of the Deployment also bypass the
      budget. Protection against involuntary failures comes from spare replicas, spreading them across nodes and zones
      (`topologySpreadConstraints`, anti-affinity) and readiness probes.
    linkTitles:
      - "Disruptions (Kubernetes docs)"
      - "API-initiated eviction (Kubernetes docs)"

    title: Which securityContext settings harden a Pod that runs an ASP.NET Core container?
    prompt: |
      A Deployment runs an ASP.NET Core service on an image based on `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0`.

    hint: Which of these settings restrict what a process inside the container can do, and which give it access to the node instead?
    options:
      a: "`runAsNonRoot: true` in the Pod-level `securityContext`"
      b: "`readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` in the container `securityContext`, plus an `emptyDir` volume mounted at `/tmp`"
      c: "`allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` in the container `securityContext`"
      d: '`capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` in the container `securityContext`'
      e: "`privileged: true` in the container `securityContext`"
      f: "`hostNetwork: true` in the Pod spec"
    optionExplanations:
      e: "A privileged container gets almost all the capabilities of processes on the node, including access to host devices. This widens privilege instead of reducing it, and the Baseline Pod Security Standard forbids it."
      f: "With `hostNetwork: true` the Pod uses the node's network namespace: it sees the node's interfaces and can listen on host ports. This widens privilege, and the Baseline Pod Security Standard forbids it."
    answer: "`runAsNonRoot: true`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` with an `emptyDir` for `/tmp`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` and `capabilities.drop: [\"ALL\"]`."
    explanation: |
      Each correct setting closes one path an attacker would use after compromising the app:

      - `runAsNonRoot: true`: the kubelet refuses to start the container if the process would run as UID 0. It can
        only verify a numeric user id. Since .NET 8 the .NET images contain the `app` user with UID 1654 (the
        `APP_UID` variable), so `USER $APP_UID` in the Dockerfile or an explicit `runAsUser: 1654` passes the check,
        while a user given only by name makes the Pod fail to start.
      - `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`: the process cannot replace the app's files or drop its own tools into the image
        file system. ASP.NET Core still needs a writable temp directory: large request bodies and uploaded files are
        buffered there, and the runtime creates its diagnostics socket there. That is why an `emptyDir` is mounted at
        `/tmp`.
      - `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` sets the `no_new_privs` flag on the process: a child process cannot gain
        more privileges than its parent, even through setuid files.
      - `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`: Kestrel on port 8080 needs no Linux capabilities, while the set the container
        runtime grants by default includes, for example, `NET_RAW` and `CHOWN`.

      `privileged: true` and `hostNetwork: true` work the other way: they give the container access to node
      resources. The Restricted Pod Security Standard requires `runAsNonRoot`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`,
      dropping all capabilities and a `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost` seccomp profile. No profile requires
      `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, but it is a common addition for stateless services.
    linkTitles:
      - "Configure a security context for a Pod or container"
      - "Pod Security Standards"

         и отставший кластер теряет поддержку), обновления образов узлов и ОС, размеры пулов узлов, проектирование

         дежурства по инцидентам кластера. Назвать, кто из шести человек будет этим заниматься, какую долю
         времени, и что будет, когда этот человек в отпуске.
      3. **Сравнить с управляемыми вариантами.** Azure Container Apps запускает контейнеры на инфраструктуре
         на базе Kubernetes, но скрывает кластер: встроенный ingress, ревизии с разделением трафика, правила
         масштабирования на базе KEDA, включая масштабирование до нуля, задания (jobs) для ночной задачи,
         управляемые удостоверения. App Service подходит для обычных HTTP-сервисов и даёт слоты развёртывания.
         Оба варианта закрывают перечисленные требования с гораздо меньшей эксплуатационной работой. AKS
         оправдан конкретной потребностью: прямой доступ к API Kubernetes, собственные операторы или CRD,
         определённый service mesh или ingress, особые конфигурации узлов, либо платформенная команда,
         которая обслуживает много команд.
      4. **Принять решение и зафиксировать его.** Вероятная рекомендация: Container Apps (или App Service для
         HTTP-сервисов) сейчас. Записать ADR с критериями, отклонёнными вариантами и явными условиями пересмотра:
         появилось требование, которому нужен API Kubernetes, команда выросла, появился платформенный инженер.

         и число инцидентов. Изучение Kubernetes вынести в учебный кластер или обучение, а не в production пяти
         сервисов, которым некому заниматься.
    explanation: |

      технологии. Управляемая плоскость управления - ещё не управляемая платформа: для команды из шести человек

  en:
    title: "A team of six wants to move five .NET services to AKS because Kubernetes is the standard: how do you choose the hosting?"
    prompt: |
      You lead a team of six developers. There is no platform engineer and no dedicated DevOps engineer.
      The team runs five .NET services: a public ASP.NET Core API, two internal HTTP services, a queue worker
      and a nightly job. Today they run on Azure virtual machines and are deployed by hand.

      The team wants to move all five services to Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), because "Kubernetes is the
      industry standard" and "it makes hiring easier". How do you make the hosting decision, and what do you propose?
    hint: Separate what the five services actually need from the reasons to want a specific platform. Who will own the platform after the move?
    answer: |
      1. **Start from requirements, not from the platform.** Write down what the services really need: HTTP
         ingress and TLS, scaling (including the queue worker scaling on queue length and running the nightly
         job), network isolation and private access to the database, zero-downtime deployment, observability,
         compliance, budget. Record the non-technical motives separately: learning Kubernetes, hiring, portability.
      2. **Price the operational ownership of AKS.** Azure manages the control plane, but the team owns:
         regular Kubernetes minor version upgrades (AKS supports a limited window of versions, and a cluster
         that falls behind loses support), node image and OS updates, node pool sizing, network design (CNI,
         address space, ingress controller, certificates), RBAC, workload identity and secrets, network
         policies, cluster monitoring, manifests or Helm charts for every service, and on-call for cluster
         incidents. Name who of the six does this, for what share of their time, and what happens when that
         person is on vacation.
      3. **Compare with the managed options.** Azure Container Apps runs containers on Kubernetes-based
         infrastructure but hides the cluster: built-in ingress, revisions with traffic splitting, KEDA-based
         scale rules including scale to zero, jobs for the nightly task, managed identities. App Service fits
         plain HTTP services and offers deployment slots. Both cover the listed requirements with far less
         operational work. AKS is justified by a concrete need: direct access to the Kubernetes API, custom
         operators or CRDs, a specific service mesh or ingress, special node configurations, or a platform
         team that serves many teams.
      4. **Decide and record it.** The likely recommendation: Container Apps (or App Service for the HTTP
         services) now. Write an ADR with the criteria, the rejected options and explicit triggers to revisit:
         a requirement that needs the Kubernetes API, team growth, a dedicated platform engineer.
      5. **Keep the way out open.** OCI images, configuration through environment variables and a secret store,
         health endpoints, OpenTelemetry, infrastructure as code. Then moving to AKS later means porting the
         deployment definitions, not rewriting the services.
      6. **Address the team's motivation.** Start with a pilot on one service and measure deployment time and
         incident count. Learning Kubernetes goes into a sandbox cluster or training, not into the production of
         five services that nobody is available to run.
    explanation: |
      The question checks whether a lead decides by total cost of ownership rather than by the popularity of a
      technology. A managed control plane is not a managed platform: for a team of six, the upgrades, networking
      and security of a cluster are recurring work that competes with product work. A cluster that nobody
      upgrades becomes both a security risk and a support problem over time.

      Container Apps and App Service move that work to Azure in exchange for less control. The trade pays off
      as long as the team does not need what only the Kubernetes API provides. Microsoft's own comparison says
      the same: if you need direct access to the Kubernetes API and control plane, choose AKS; otherwise Container
      Apps covers most microservice scenarios.

      The decision is also cheap to reverse if the services are built as portable containers, so there is no
      need to pay for Kubernetes today "just in case". A strong answer does not dismiss the team's wish: it turns
      "industry standard" into checkable criteria and conditions under which the decision is revisited.
    linkTitles:
      - "Comparing Container Apps with other Azure container options"
      - "Choose an Azure compute service"
      - "Supported Kubernetes versions in AKS"

  en:
    title: "Two months after enabling autoscaling the cloud bill has doubled: what do you do?"
    prompt: |
      Two months ago pod and node autoscaling was enabled for your .NET services in Kubernetes. Since then the
      cloud bill has roughly doubled. The finance department asks you, as the tech lead, to explain where the
      growth comes from and to propose a plan.

      What do you do, and in what order?
    hint: What is actually billed - the CPU that is used, or the capacity that is provisioned? And what in the cluster decides how much capacity is provisioned?
    answer: |
      1. **Do not switch autoscaling off blindly, and agree on a timeline.** Tell finance there will be an analysis
         with numbers and a plan with expected savings by a clear date. A sudden shutdown saves money at the cost of
         availability, and nobody yet knows what actually grew.
      2. **Attribute the cost.** Break the bill down by tags, resource groups or accounts, and inside a shared
         cluster by namespace and service (Kubernetes cost allocation tools such as OpenCost). Overlay scaling
         events on the cost graph: replica count, node count and traffic. The key question: did the cost per unit
         of work (per 1000 requests, per processed message) grow, or did traffic simply grow? Resources without tags
         and without an owner are already a finding.
      3. **Find the causes.** Typical ones:
         - oversized `requests`: the scheduler places pods by `requests`, not by real usage, so the cluster
           autoscaler adds nodes for reserved but idle capacity;
         - no sensible cap: the HPA `maxReplicas` or the node pool maximum is set "with headroom", and a load spike
           or a retry storm inflates the cluster;
         - scale-in never happens: a high `minReplicas`, a target utilization that is too low, a metric that barely
           drops (for example the memory of a .NET process that is in no hurry to return its heap to the OS), or pods
           that prevent the cluster autoscaler from removing a node;
         - the wrong signal: CPU spikes from pod startup during deployments, or retries, trigger scaling;
         - test environments scale like production and run around the clock;
         - indirect costs: more replicas mean more logs and telemetry, more sidecars, more egress and more
           database connections.
      4. **Fix one change at a time and measure.** Size `requests` to observed usage, set replica and node caps
         based on what the dependencies can absorb, tune targets and stabilization windows, and use scale to zero
         or schedules for non-production environments. Cover the steady baseline with reservations or savings
         plans, and move interruptible workloads to spot nodes. Check latency and error rate after each step.
      5. **Make cost an engineering metric.** Budgets and alerts (Azure Cost Management, AWS Budgets), anomaly
         alerts, mandatory owner tags enforced by policy, cost per unit of work on the team dashboard, and a regular
         cost review. Every service has a budget owner, and changes to scaling limits go through code review.
      6. **Report back.** Give finance an explanation with numbers: which part of the growth is business growth and
         which is misconfiguration, plus a plan with expected savings, dates and honestly stated reliability
         trade-offs.
    explanation: |
      Autoscaling optimizes the signal it is given, not cost. The bill is for provisioned capacity: nodes,
      instances, replicas. In Kubernetes provisioned capacity follows `requests`, because the scheduler reserves for
      a pod exactly what its `requests` say. So a service at 20% CPU with oversized `requests` can need twice the
      nodes it actually uses.

      Scaling is also asymmetric: it goes up quickly and comes down cautiously, with stabilization windows that
      prevent flapping. With poorly chosen targets, caps and metrics the cluster easily "sticks" at the top, and
      cost grows without any growth in traffic.

      The lead's job here is not only technical. You resist both the urge to "turn it all off" and blind trust in
      automation, and first separate business growth from configuration waste. Caps carry risk too: a limit that is
      too low causes an outage at a real peak, so it is derived from the capacity of the dependencies and has an
      alert when it is reached. The lasting result comes when cost has owners, budgets and alerts, and is watched
      next to latency and errors instead of being discovered from an email from finance.
    linkTitles:
      - "Azure Well-Architected Framework: cost optimization"
      - "Resource management for pods and containers (Kubernetes docs)"

  en:
    title: How do you choose a secrets management approach for several teams on a shared Kubernetes cluster?
    prompt: |
      Five teams deploy their .NET services to one shared AKS cluster. Today every team does it differently: some keep
      YAML with `Secret` objects in Git, some inject passwords into environment variables from the CI pipeline, and
      some put connection strings straight into `appsettings.Production.json`. As the lead you are asked to propose a
      single approach.

      How do you choose the way secrets are managed, what do you make the standard for all teams, and what does it
      depend on?
    hint: A Kubernetes `Secret` is a way to deliver a value to a Pod. Where is the master copy of the secret then, who rotates it, and who sees that it was accessed?
    answer: |
      1. **Start with requirements, not a tool.** Who owns the secrets (the service team or the platform), how often
         they must be rotated, whether access auditing is required by security or a regulator, whether GitOps is used,
         whether portability across clouds matters. This decides whether built-in `Secret` objects are enough or an
         external store is needed.
      2. **The master copy lives in an external store.** For several teams a reasonable standard is Azure Key Vault as
         the source of truth: a separate vault per team and environment, permissions through Azure RBAC, an access log,
         versions and rotation in one place. Pods access it through Microsoft Entra Workload ID bound to a service
         account, with no long-lived passwords or keys in the cluster.
      3. **Delivery into the Pod.** The Secrets Store CSI Driver with the Azure Key Vault provider: a team describes a
         `SecretProviderClass`, and secrets are mounted into the container as files. Enable syncing into a `Secret`
         object only where environment variables are really needed: that object again needs the same protection as a
         plain `Secret`. Alternatives are the External Secrets Operator (creates `Secret` objects from the external
         store) or the app reading Key Vault itself through a configuration provider; one choice is fixed for everyone.
      4. **If plain `Secret` objects remain.** Encryption of etcd at rest, least-privilege RBAC (`list` and `watch`
         permissions on secrets effectively reveal their values), a separate namespace per team, because anyone who can
         create a Pod in a namespace can read any `Secret` in that namespace. Values never go into Git in plain form;
         for GitOps only encrypted forms (for example Sealed Secrets or SOPS).
      5. **The .NET side.** Mounted files are read by the key-per-file configuration provider (`AddKeyPerFile`): the
         file name becomes the key, and `ConnectionStrings__Main` becomes `ConnectionStrings:Main`. Environment
         variables do not change on rotation until the Pod restarts; files are updated, but the app must re-read the
         configuration or recreate connections. Rotation is designed so that the old and new values are both valid for
         a while.
      6. **Make it a process.** A template (a "paved road") for new services, a cluster policy that blocks workarounds,
         regular review of access logs, a runbook for rotation and for responding to a leak, a clear owner for every
         secret. Exceptions are allowed but recorded with a reason.
    explanation: |
      The key idea: a Kubernetes `Secret` solves delivering a value to a Pod, not managing the secret. It has no
      central rotation, no version history and no convenient audit across teams, and by default it is only
      base64-encoded. So with several teams the master copy moves to a store that does all of this itself, and the
      cluster only receives a synced copy. A vault per team and environment limits the blast radius of a permission
      mistake or a leak.

      This has a cost the lead should state honestly: an external dependency (if the store is unreachable when a Pod
      starts, the volume is not mounted and the Pod does not start), a driver or operator that must be upgraded and
      monitored, and extra identity setup. For one small team with rare rotation, built-in `Secret` objects with etcd
      encryption and strict RBAC may be enough.

      A separate management part is consistency. Five different ways mean five places where a password can leak and
      five rotation procedures. One standard path, enforced by a template and policies, reduces risk more than picking
      the "perfect" tool.
    linkTitles:
      - "Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets"
      - "Use the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver in an AKS cluster"

    title: "Общий кластер Kubernetes с пространствами имён или отдельные кластеры: как выбрать топологию для 40 сервисов и 8 команд?"
    prompt: |
      Компания запускает в Kubernetes 40 сервисов на .NET, которыми владеют 8 команд. Одни предлагают один
      общий кластер, где у каждой команды своё пространство имён. Другие - отдельный кластер на каждую команду

         `NetworkPolicy` и Pod Security Admission. Всё это нужно настроить явно: без политик поды разных
         пространств имён свободно ходят друг к другу по сети, а квот нет. Общими остаются плоскость управления

         версия Kubernetes и её обновления, а на общих узлах - ещё и ядро ОС.
      2. **Что даёт отдельный кластер.** Жёсткую изоляцию: свой API-сервер, свои обновления, свои учётные данные
         и сетевые границы; сбой или ошибка конфигурации остаются внутри. Цена - дублирование эксплуатации:
         обновления версий, дополнения (контроллер ingress, мониторинг, агенты политик), доступы, резерв мощности
         на узлах в каждом кластере.
      3. **Критерии.** Степень доверия между арендаторами (свои команды одной компании или чужой код), требования
         соответствия и аудита (PCI DSS, персональные данные, размещение данных), допустимый радиус поражения

      where every team gets its own namespace. Others propose a separate cluster per team or per environment.

      How do you make the decision? Which criteria matter, which topology do you propose by default, and in which
      cases do you set up a separate cluster?
    hint: What exactly stays shared by all tenants of one cluster, and what does a namespace on its own not protect against?
    answer: |
      1. **What a namespace gives.** Soft isolation: it is the boundary for RBAC, `ResourceQuota` and `LimitRange`,
         `NetworkPolicy` and Pod Security Admission. All of this must be configured explicitly: without policies,
         Pods in different namespaces reach each other freely over the network, and there are no quotas. What stays
         shared is the control plane (API server, etcd), cluster-scoped objects (CRDs, `ClusterRole`, admission
         webhooks, `StorageClass`), the Kubernetes version and its upgrades, and on shared nodes also the OS kernel.
      2. **What a separate cluster gives.** Hard isolation: its own API server, its own upgrades, its own
         credentials and network boundaries; a failure or a misconfiguration stays inside. The price is duplicated
         operations: version upgrades, add-ons (ingress controller, monitoring, policy agents), access management,
         spare node capacity in every cluster.
      3. **Criteria.** The level of trust between tenants (teams of one company or foreign code), compliance and
         audit requirements (PCI DSS, personal data, data residency), the acceptable blast radius (a failed upgrade,
         a broken admission webhook or an overloaded API server hits everyone), the need for cluster-level rights
         (own operators and CRDs, a different Kubernetes version), and the cost and maturity of the platform team.
         The number of teams is not a criterion on its own.
      4. **Default layout.** Production is separated from non-production by different clusters, and if needed
         there is one cluster per region. Inside a cluster there is a namespace per team or per service: RBAC by
         groups from the identity provider, quotas and default resource values, a default-deny `NetworkPolicy`,
         the `restricted` profile of the Pod Security Standards, and dedicated node pools through taints and
         tolerations where needed. Namespaces are created from templates through GitOps, so a new tenant gets all
         the guardrails at once.
      5. **When a separate cluster is needed.** Regulated data and external audit, untrusted code (for example,
         customer code), availability requirements that must not depend on other teams' changes, cluster-level
         components that conflict with the shared ones.
      6. **What to avoid.** A cluster per team "just in case": 8 teams times 2-3 environments is 16-24 clusters to
         upgrade and maintain. And one cluster for production and test environments, where an experiment in a test
         namespace can overload the shared API server or nodes.
    explanation: |
      The Kubernetes documentation distinguishes soft multi-tenancy, where tenants mostly trust each other (teams
      of one organization), from hard multi-tenancy, where there is no such trust. A namespace is a tool for the
      soft kind: it separates API access and resources, but the control plane, cluster-scoped objects and nodes
      stay shared. Isolation is therefore built from several layers, and each one must be turned on and maintained:
      a namespace without RBAC, quotas and network policies isolates almost nothing.

      A separate cluster removes these risks, but every cluster is one more thing to operate. Managed services
      (AKS, EKS) take over the control plane, but not the version upgrades, add-ons, policies and observability in
      each cluster. Between the two extremes there are middle options: dedicated node pools for sensitive workloads,
      or a virtual control plane per tenant on top of a shared cluster.

      So the cluster boundary is drawn where the boundary of trust, compliance or acceptable blast radius lies, not
      along the org chart. Teams change more often than isolation requirements, and a cluster per team turns every
      reorganization into a migration. The decision is worth recording as an architecture decision (ADR) and
      revisiting when new requirements appear, such as regulated data.
    linkTitles:
      - "Multi-tenancy (Kubernetes docs)"
      - "Best practices for cluster isolation in Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)"

    title: What does a feature flag (release toggle) change about shipping unfinished functionality to production?
    prompt: |
      A team builds functionality that will take several weeks of work and does not want to keep it in a
      long-lived branch. The code is merged into the main branch regularly and deployed to production, but it is
      hidden behind a release feature flag (release toggle). Which statement correctly describes what such a flag changes?
    hint: Think about when the code reaches the servers, when users see it, and what happens to the flag itself afterwards.
    options:
      a: "Deployment is separated from release: the unfinished code already runs in production switched off, and it can be turned on for users later by flipping the flag, without deploying a new version of the code. The flag and the old code path are temporary debt that must be removed after the release."
      b: "Users cannot see code behind a disabled flag, so it does not need tests or a pipeline run: it only has to be checked at the moment the flag is turned on."

    answer: "The flag separates deployment from release: the code is deployed switched off and turned on for users later without deploying new code, and the flag must be removed after the release."

      So unfinished work has to live in a separate branch, and long-lived branches lead to painful merges.

      A release flag pulls these events apart. Unfinished code is merged into the main branch and deployed with
      everything else, but only the `if` branch chosen by the flag runs. When the functionality is ready, it is
      turned on by flipping the flag, for everyone at once or gradually for a share of users. If something goes
      wrong, the flag is turned off just as fast, without rolling back the deployment.

      The approach has a cost. Every flag adds a branch to the code and doubles the number of paths to test. That
      is why release flags must be short-lived: a removal task or an expiry date is created together with the
      flag, and after the release both the flag and the old code path are deleted. Otherwise flags pile up as
      technical debt.

locales:
  ru:
    title: Какие проверки должен запускать CI .NET-сервиса на каждый pull request и в каком порядке?
    prompt: |
      Команда настраивает конвейер непрерывной интеграции для .NET-сервиса. Какие проверки он должен выполнять
      на каждый pull request, в каком порядке их расположить и почему именно так? При каком условии pull request
      можно сливать?
    hint: Какая проверка самая дешёвая, и какой шаг бессмысленно запускать, пока не прошёл предыдущий?
    answer: |
      Порядок строится по принципу «сначала дешёвое и быстрое»: чем раньше падает проверка, тем быстрее автор
      получает ответ и тем меньше ресурсов CI потрачено зря.

      1. **Окружение.** Версия SDK закреплена в `global.json`, и CI ставит именно её (например, `actions/setup-dotnet`
         умеет взять версию из `global.json`). Конвейер проверяет результат слияния с целевой веткой, а не только
         ветку автора.
      2. **Восстановление пакетов** `dotnet restore --locked-mode`. При включённом `RestorePackagesWithLockFile`
         восстановление падает, если `packages.lock.json` не соответствует проектам, поэтому зависимости
         воспроизводимы. Папка пакетов NuGet кэшируется с ключом по хешу lock-файлов. Здесь же уместна проверка
         уязвимых зависимостей (NuGet Audit или `dotnet list package --vulnerable`).
      3. **Форматирование** `dotnet format --verify-no-changes`. Занимает секунды и падает, если код не
         соответствует `.editorconfig`, так что спор о стиле не доходит до code review.
      4. **Сборка** `dotnet build --no-restore -c Release -warnaserror` (или `TreatWarningsAsErrors` в
         `Directory.Build.props`). Компилятор и анализаторы работают здесь, а предупреждения не копятся.
      5. **Модульные тесты** `dotnet test --no-build -c Release`. Быстрые и без внешних зависимостей, отчёт
         публикуется в pull request.
      6. **Интеграционные тесты.** Медленнее, с настоящей базой в контейнере. Их можно запускать отдельным
         параллельным заданием после сборки.
      7. **Публикация одного артефакта** `dotnet publish --no-build -c Release` и загрузка результата (или образа
         контейнера). Именно этот артефакт затем продвигается по окружениям, а не пересобирается для каждого.
      8. **Правило слияния.** Все шаги - обязательные проверки в защите ветки (branch protection): pull request
         сливается только при зелёном конвейере, без ручных исключений.
    explanation: |
      Порядок следует из стоимости и зависимостей шагов. Если не восстановились пакеты, всё остальное
      бессмысленно. Проверка форматирования стоит секунды, сборка - минуту, тесты - дольше всего, поэтому дешёвые

      тесты проверяют те самые двоичные файлы, которые потом публикуются: сборка выполняется один раз.

      Фаулер в статье о непрерывной интеграции подчёркивает две вещи: сборка должна быть быстрой (ориентир -
      около десяти минут), а основная ветка должна всегда оставаться рабочей. Поэтому медленные проверки

  en:
    title: Which checks should the CI of a .NET service run on every pull request, and in what order?
    prompt: |
      A team sets up a continuous integration pipeline for a .NET service. Which checks should it run on every
      pull request, in what order should they go, and why that order? Under which condition may the pull request

    hint: Which check is the cheapest, and which step is pointless to run until the previous one has passed?
    answer: |
      The order follows the rule "cheap and fast first": the earlier a check fails, the sooner the author gets

         example, `actions/setup-dotnet` can read it from `global.json`). The pipeline checks the result of merging
         with the target branch, not only the author's branch.
      2. **Package restore** with `dotnet restore --locked-mode`. With `RestorePackagesWithLockFile` enabled, restore
         fails if `packages.lock.json` does not match the projects, so dependencies are reproducible. The NuGet
         packages folder is cached with a key based on the hash of the lock files. A check for vulnerable
         dependencies fits here too (NuGet Audit or `dotnet list package --vulnerable`).
      3. **Formatting** with `dotnet format --verify-no-changes`. It takes seconds and fails when the code does not
         match `.editorconfig`, so style arguments never reach code review.
      4. **Build** with `dotnet build --no-restore -c Release -warnaserror` (or `TreatWarningsAsErrors` in
         `Directory.Build.props`). The compiler and analyzers run here, and warnings do not pile up.
      5. **Unit tests** with `dotnet test --no-build -c Release`. Fast and free of external dependencies; the
         report is published to the pull request.
      6. **Integration tests.** Slower, with a real database in a container. They can run as a separate parallel
         job after the build.
      7. **Publish one artifact** with `dotnet publish --no-build -c Release` and upload the result (or a container
         image). This artifact is then promoted through the environments instead of being rebuilt for each.
      8. **Merge rule.** Every step is a required check in branch protection: the pull request merges only when the
         pipeline is green, with no manual exceptions.
    explanation: |
      The order comes from the cost and the dependencies of the steps. If packages did not restore, nothing else
      makes sense. The format check costs seconds, the build about a minute, tests the longest, so the cheap checks
      go first and stop the pipeline earlier. The `--no-restore` and `--no-build` switches guarantee that the tests
      check the very binaries that are published later: the build happens once.

      In his article on continuous integration Fowler stresses two things: the build must be fast (the guideline
      is about ten minutes), and the mainline must always stay healthy. That is why slow checks are parallelised or
      moved to separate jobs, and merging without a green pipeline is blocked technically, not by agreement.

      Common mistakes: rebuilding the project at every step (slower, and what is tested is not what is published),
      restoring packages without a lock file (the build depends on whatever the NuGet feed serves today), and
      publishing the artifact before the tests pass.

    title: Почему активность Health получает родителя Import, хотя должна быть корневой?
    prompt: |
      В программе зарегистрирован `ActivityListener`, который записывает все активности источника `Shop.Jobs`.
      Метод `RunImport` начинает активность `Import`. Затем программа начинает активность `Health`, которая
      должна быть корневой, и печатает имя её родителя или `root`, если родителя нет. Ожидается `root`, но
      программа печатает `Import`. Щёлкните по строке с дефектом.

    answer: |
      Строка 14: активность `Import` создаётся без `using` и никогда не останавливается, поэтому остаётся в
      `Activity.Current` и становится родителем `Health`.
    explanation: |
      `ActivitySource.StartActivity` не только создаёт активность, но и запускает её, а запуск делает её текущей:
      `Activity.Current` теперь указывает на `Import`. Значение хранится в `AsyncLocal`, и вернуть прежнее может
      только остановка активности (`Stop`, которую вызывает `Dispose`). В строке 14 активность никто не
      останавливает. Метод `RunImport` синхронный, поэтому изменение `Activity.Current` остаётся видимым
      вызывающему коду и после выхода из метода. Когда `StartActivity("Health")` вызывается без явного
      родительского контекста, родителем становится `Activity.Current`, то есть `Import`, и программа печатает

      В сервисе последствия хуже, чем неверный родитель. Все последующие спаны в этом потоке выполнения
      попадают в чужую трассировку. А сам `Import` никогда не завершается: слушатели не получают
      `ActivityStopped`, поэтому экспортёр OpenTelemetry его не отправит, и у спана не будет длительности.

      Исправление - объявление `using`: в конце `RunImport` вызывается `Dispose`, активность останавливается и
      `Activity.Current` возвращается к прежнему значению (`null`). Тогда `Health` становится корневой, и
      программа печатает `root`. Строка 15 корректна: `?.` нужен на случай, когда слушателей нет и
      `StartActivity` возвращает `null`. Поведение описано для .NET 10.

      - "Свойство Activity.Current"
      - "Добавление распределённой трассировки в .NET: пошаговые примеры"
  en:
    title: Why does the Health activity get Import as its parent when it should be a root?
    prompt: |
      The program registers an `ActivityListener` that records every activity of the `Shop.Jobs` source. The
      `RunImport` method starts an `Import` activity. Then the program starts a `Health` activity, which should be
      a root, and prints the name of its parent, or `root` when there is no parent. It should print `root`, but it
      prints `Import`. Click the line that contains the defect.
    hint: Where does `StartActivity("Health")` take its parent from when no parent context is passed explicitly?
    answer: |
      Line 14: the `Import` activity is created without `using` and is never stopped, so it stays in
      `Activity.Current` and becomes the parent of `Health`.
    explanation: |
      `ActivitySource.StartActivity` does not only create an activity, it also starts it, and starting makes it
      current: `Activity.Current` now points to `Import`. The value is stored in an `AsyncLocal`, and only stopping
      the activity (`Stop`, which `Dispose` calls) restores the previous one. On line 14 nobody stops the activity.
      `RunImport` is a synchronous method, so the change to `Activity.Current` stays visible to the caller after
      the method returns. When `StartActivity("Health")` is called without an explicit parent context, the parent
      is `Activity.Current`, that is `Import`, and the program prints `Import`.

      In a service the consequences are worse than a wrong parent. Every later span in that execution flow ends up
      in someone else's trace. And `Import` itself never ends: listeners never get `ActivityStopped`, so the
      OpenTelemetry exporter never sends it, and the span has no duration.

      The fix is a `using` declaration: `Dispose` runs at the end of `RunImport`, the activity stops and
      `Activity.Current` returns to its previous value (`null`). Then `Health` becomes a root and the program
      prints `root`. Line 15 is fine: `?.` covers the case when there are no listeners and `StartActivity` returns
      `null`. The behaviour is described for .NET 10.

      - "Activity.Current property"
      - "Adding distributed tracing instrumentation: walkthroughs"

    title: Why does a LogDebug call allocate even when the Debug level is disabled?
    prompt: |
      In a .NET 10 service a hot path processes tens of thousands of items per second and calls
      `_logger.LogDebug("Item {Id} at {Price}", id, price)` for each one, where `id` is an `int` and `price` is a
      `decimal`. In production the minimum log level is `Information`, so `Debug` entries go nowhere. Still, a memory
      profiler shows allocations of `object[]`, `Int32` and `Decimal` at this call. Which statement correctly
      explains the cause and how to remove it?
    hint: Look at the signature of `LogDebug` - what are the types of its parameters, and what must the compiler do with the arguments before the method is even entered?
    options:
      a: 'The logger puts `id` and `price` into the template and builds the message string before checking the level, then throws it away. Interpolation `$"Item {id} at {price}"` helps because it formats the string without parsing a template.'
      b: '`LogDebug` is declared as `LogDebug(this ILogger logger, string? message, params object?[] args)`, so an `object[]` array and the boxed `int` and `decimal` are created at the call site before the level is checked. A method generated with `[LoggerMessage]`, or a `_logger.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Debug)` check before the call, removes the cost.'
      c: 'The template string `"Item {Id} at {Price}"` is allocated again on every call. Moving the template into a `const string` field helps.'
      d: 'The cost disappears if the configuration sets the level of this category to `None`: the logger then skips the call entirely and the arguments are not evaluated.'
    optionExplanations:
      a: 'When the level is disabled, no message string is built: the logger checks the level before it calls the formatter. Interpolation does the opposite: it builds the string on every call, before `LogDebug` is entered, and also loses the structured properties `Id` and `Price`.'
      c: 'A string literal is a single interned instance and is not allocated on every call. `const` changes nothing at run time: the array and the boxed values are still created.'
      d: 'The level filter runs inside the logger at run time. The `params` array and the boxing are done by the calling code before `LogDebug` is entered, so the level setting does not remove them. This is not `[Conditional]`: the call stays in the compiled code.'
    answer: 'The `LoggerExtensions` methods take `params object?[]`, so the array and the boxed `int` and `decimal` are created at the call site before the level check. A method generated with `[LoggerMessage]`, or an `IsEnabled` check before the call, removes the cost.'
    explanation: |
      The extension method `LoggerExtensions.LogDebug(this ILogger logger, string? message, params object?[] args)`
      receives its arguments as `params object?[]`. The compiler turns the call into the creation of a two-element
      array, and since `int` and `decimal` are value types, each one is boxed into a separate heap object. All of

      API на ASP.NET Core принимает HTTP-запрос и публикует сообщение в брокер (RabbitMQ, Kafka, Azure Service Bus).

         инструментированы, контекст в сообщение никто не записывает. В `BackgroundService` worker-а нет
         `Activity.Current`, поэтому `StartActivity` начинает новую корневую трассу.
      2. **Producer: записать контекст в заголовки сообщения.** При публикации стартует спан с
         `ActivityKind.Producer` (например, `send orders`), и его контекст записывается в заголовки сообщения в том же
         формате W3C: `DistributedContextPropagator.Current.Inject(activity, headers, setter)` или
         `Propagators.DefaultTextMapPropagator.Inject(...)` из OpenTelemetry. Контекст принадлежит сообщению, а не
         соединению: он переживает повторы, повторную доставку и попадание в dead-letter queue. При использовании
         outbox заголовки надо сохранить в строку outbox в той же транзакции: ретранслятор публикует сообщение позже и
         в другом контексте.

         `messaging.system`, `messaging.destination.name`, идентификатор сообщения.

         трасс. Если взять родителем первое сообщение, остальные 49 трасс потеряют свою обработку, а выбранная трасса
         покажет чужую работу. Поэтому спан пакета - корневой (или дочерний к собственному спану цикла чтения
         worker-а) и несёт по одной `ActivityLink` на контекст каждого сообщения, плюс атрибут

  en:
    title: How do you keep one distributed trace through a message broker, and how do you trace batch processing?
    prompt: |
      An ASP.NET Core API receives an HTTP request and publishes a message to a broker (RabbitMQ, Kafka, Azure
      Service Bus). A separate worker service reads the message and processes it. In the tracing backend the API
      request and the worker processing show up as two unrelated traces.

      Why does this happen, and how do you link them into one trace? How do you model the spans when the consumer
      fetches and processes messages in batches, for example 50 at a time?
    hint: How does trace context get from one HTTP service to another, and what can play that role for a message? How many parents can one span have?
    answer: |
      1. **Why the trace breaks.** ASP.NET Core and `HttpClient` propagate context only over HTTP: the outgoing
         request gets a `traceparent` header (plus `tracestate` and baggage), and the server reads it and makes its
         span a child. A broker is not HTTP. Unless the broker client library or messaging framework is
         instrumented, nobody writes the context into the message. The worker's `BackgroundService` has no
         `Activity.Current`, so `StartActivity` begins a new root trace.
      2. **Producer: write the context into the message headers.** When publishing, start a span with
         `ActivityKind.Producer` (for example `send orders`) and write its context into the message headers in the
         same W3C format: `DistributedContextPropagator.Current.Inject(activity, headers, setter)` or
         `Propagators.DefaultTextMapPropagator.Inject(...)` from OpenTelemetry. The context belongs to the message,
         not the connection: it survives retries, redelivery and a trip to the dead-letter queue. With an outbox,
         store the headers in the outbox row in the same transaction: the relay publishes the message later and in
         another context.
      3. **Consumer: extract the context and start a span from it.** For each message the worker reads the headers,
         parses them (`DistributedContextPropagator.Current.ExtractTraceIdAndState` and `ActivityContext.TryParse`,
         or `Extract` on the OpenTelemetry propagator) and starts a span with `ActivityKind.Consumer` and that
         parent: `source.StartActivity("process orders", ActivityKind.Consumer, parentContext)`. Everything the
         handler does (EF Core, `HttpClient`) becomes its descendants, and the trace goes API -> broker -> worker.
         Register the source with `AddSource`, and give the spans semantic convention attributes:
         `messaging.system`, `messaging.destination.name`, the message id.
      4. **Batch: links instead of a parent.** A span has only one parent, but the 50 messages of a batch came from
         50 different traces. If the first message becomes the parent, the other 49 traces lose their processing
         and the chosen trace shows work that is not its own. So the batch span is a root (or a child of the
         worker's own polling span) and carries one `ActivityLink` per message context, plus the
         `messaging.batch.message_count` attribute. Links are passed at start through the `links` parameter of
         `StartActivity`, so the sampler sees them; .NET 9 also added `Activity.AddLink`. If messages inside the
         batch are handled one by one, you can additionally start a span per message whose parent is that message's
         context, so every original trace shows its own part of the work.
      5. **Cost and verification.**
         - Traces connected by links stay separate: the backend shows a jump through the link, not one tree.
         - Their sampling decisions are independent: `ParentBasedSampler` follows the parent, not the links, so the
           linked producer trace may not be kept.
         - If a message waits in the queue for hours, a trace with a parent stretches over hours; some teams use
           links even for single messages for that reason.
         - The messaging semantic conventions are still in development status and attribute names changed between
           versions, so pin the conventions version.
         - An integration test: publish a message and check that the consumer span has the same `TraceId` as the
           producer span, or a link to it.
    explanation: |
      Context propagation is not a property of the network but an application-level agreement: the sender puts the
      context into a carrier, and the receiver takes it out. For HTTP the carrier is the request headers, and the
      built-in instrumentation does the work. For a broker the carrier must be the message headers (properties),
      and as long as nobody fills and reads them, the traces are not connected. The format is the same W3C Trace
      Context, so the standard propagator is enough.

      Batch processing runs into the trace model: a tree allows one parent. That is why the OpenTelemetry messaging
      semantic conventions describe the message creation context and span links: one span is honestly connected to
      every trace its messages came from, and none of those traces claims work that is not its own.

      Typical mistakes: relying on `Activity.Current` in a background worker, passing only the `TraceId` without
      the `SpanId` and flags, making the first message of a batch the parent, and forgetting the outbox, where
      publishing is separated from the original request. The API behaviour is described for .NET 10;
      `Activity.AddLink` is available since .NET 9.
    linkTitles:
      - "OpenTelemetry: semantic conventions for messaging spans"
      - "Distributed tracing concepts in .NET"
      - "DistributedContextPropagator class"

         вместо записи на каждый элемент, а если запись по сути считает события - заменить её счётчиком `Counter<T>`
         из `System.Diagnostics.Metrics`. После выкатки исправления убрать временное правило из конфигурации.
      7. **Не допустить повторения.**
         - Алерт на резкий рост объёма логов по сервису и категории и алерт на расходы в бэкенде логов.
         - Правило для code review: `Information` - для значимых событий, а не для каждого элемента в цикле или
           каждой итерации опроса.
         - Сравнение объёма логов новой и предыдущей версии при постепенной выкатке и число записей на запрос в
           нагрузочном тесте.
         - Разбор инцидента без поиска виноватых, с этими действиями в виде задач.
    explanation: |
      Сначала измерение, потом действие: без группировки по категории и шаблону легко заглушить не то или пропустить,
      что лог - лишь видимая часть дефекта.

      Фильтр по категории - самое узкое и дешёвое средство. Проверка уровня выполняется в приложении до

      Но фильтр - временная мера: он прячет симптом и остаётся в конфигурации неочевидным знанием. Поэтому
      исправляется сам вызов, а алерты на объём и правила ревью закрывают причину, по которой проблему первым
      заметил счёт, а не мониторинг.

  en:
    title: "After a release the logging bill tripled because of millions of Information entries: what do you do now and afterwards?"
    prompt: |
      After a release the bill for log ingestion and storage tripled. It turns out that one .NET service writes
      millions of `Information` entries per minute. Users see no errors and the service responds normally.

      What do you do right now to stop the costs from growing, and what do you do afterwards so that it does not
      happen again?
    hint: "Where in the application is it decided whether an entry gets written, and can that decision change without a new release?"
    answer: |
      1. **Find the source.** In the log backend, group the service's entries for the last hour by category (the
         logger name, usually the full type name from `ILogger<T>`) and by message template (`{OriginalFormat}`) or
         `EventId`. Usually one or two templates account for almost all of the volume. Use the template to find the
         line of code and the commit that added it.
      2. **Make sure it is not a symptom.** Millions of identical entries may mean not a chatty log but a defect:
         endless reprocessing of a message, retries without delay, a polling loop without a pause. Check the metrics
         of CPU, dependency calls and queues. If the behaviour is broken, the right step is rolling back the release,
         not a filter.
      3. **Raise the minimum level for this category only.** Add the key `Logging:LogLevel:Shop.Orders.SyncWorker`
         with the value `Warning` (the category name comes from step 1). For each provider the rule with the longest
         matching category prefix is chosen, so other categories keep writing `Information`. Do not lower `Default`
         for the whole service: you lose context you will need in the next incident.
      4. **Apply it without a redeploy.** Logging filters watch for changes through
         `IOptionsMonitor<LoggerFilterOptions>`, so the new rule takes effect at once if the configuration source
         reloads: a JSON file with `reloadOnChange: true` (this is how the default host adds `appsettings.json`), a
         mounted volume with a configuration file, or an external source with refresh, such as Azure App
         Configuration. Environment variables and command-line arguments are read at startup, so changing them
         requires restarting the instances, and `AddFilter` rules in code require a new release. After the change,
         check on the graph that the flow of entries dropped.
      5. **If the application cannot be changed quickly,** drop this category's entries in the delivery pipeline
         (the collection agent, an OpenTelemetry Collector) before the backend. That stops the bill from growing, but
         the service still spends CPU and network on formatting and sending.
      6. **Afterwards, fix the code itself.** Move the entry to `Debug` or `Trace`, write one summary entry per batch
         instead of one per item, and if the entry is really counting events, replace it with a `Counter<T>` from
         `System.Diagnostics.Metrics`. Once the fix is deployed, remove the temporary rule from configuration.
      7. **Prevent a repeat.**
         - An alert on a sharp growth of log volume per service and category, and a cost alert in the log backend.
         - A code review rule: `Information` is for significant events, not for every item in a loop or every
           polling iteration.
         - Comparing the log volume of the next and the previous version during a gradual rollout, and the number of
           entries per request in a load test.
         - A blameless incident review with these actions as tasks.
    explanation: |
      Measure first, act second: without grouping by category and template it is easy to silence the wrong thing or
      miss that the log is only the visible part of a defect.

      A category filter is the narrowest and cheapest tool. The level check runs in the application before the
      entry is formatted and sent, so it saves not only storage but also CPU, network and backend ingestion. It can
      be applied in minutes, while a release with a fix goes through the pipeline, review and rollout, and every
      minute of waiting costs money. That is exactly why log levels should live in reloadable configuration, not in
      code.

      But the filter is a temporary measure: it hides the symptom and stays in configuration as non-obvious
      knowledge. So the call itself gets fixed, and volume alerts and review rules address the reason why the bill,
      not the monitoring, noticed the problem first.
    linkTitles:
      - "Logging in C# and .NET"
      - "Configuration providers in .NET"

locales:
  ru:
    title: "Релиз раз в месяц в пятницу вечером почти всегда требует хотфикса: что вы измените как техлид?"
    prompt: |
      Ваша команда выпускает сервис на .NET раз в месяц, в пятницу вечером. Перед выкладкой выполняется длинный
      ручной чек-лист. Тем не менее после большинства релизов приходится срочно выпускать хотфикс. Вы техлид.

      Что вы измените, в каком порядке и как поймёте, что изменения работают?
    hint: Что растёт вместе с интервалом между релизами и как это влияет на поиск причины, когда после выкладки что-то сломалось?
    answer: |
      1. **Собрать факты, а не мнения.** По последним нескольким релизам выяснить:
         - сколько изменений (задач, pull request) входило в каждый релиз;
         - сколько хотфиксов понадобилось и чем был вызван каждый;
         - какие пункты чек-листа занимают больше всего времени и где чаще всего ошибаются.

         Зафиксировать исходные значения метрик DORA: время выполнения изменений (от коммита до production),
         частоту развёртываний, долю неудачных изменений (здесь это доля релизов с хотфиксом или откатом) и время
         восстановления после неудачного развёртывания.
      2. **Назвать настоящую причину.** Дело не в людях и не в нехватке проверок, а в размере партии. За месяц
         накапливаются десятки изменений, они взаимодействуют друг с другом, и когда что-то ломается, трудно понять,
         какое изменение виновато. Обратная связь приходит через недели после того, как код написан. Длинный ручной
         чек-лист редко выполняется одинаково. Пятница вечером добавляет усталость и выходные, когда рядом нет
         людей, знающих изменения.
      3. **Сразу уменьшить ущерб, ничего не перестраивая.** Перенести выкладку на утро рабочего дня в середине
         недели, когда вся команда на месте. Для каждого релиза заранее определить ответственного и способ отката.
         Это не лечит причину, но снижает цену сбоев, пока идёт основная работа.
      4. **Превратить чек-лист в конвейер.** Каждый пункт чек-листа - кандидат на автоматизацию: сборка одного
         артефакта, тесты, применение миграций, развёртывание, smoke-тесты после выкладки, откат на предыдущий
         артефакт. Начинать с пунктов, где чаще всего ошибаются или которые дольше всего выполняются. То, что пока
         нельзя автоматизировать, остаётся коротким явным списком.
      5. **Уменьшать партию по шагам.** Перейти на релиз раз в две недели, затем раз в неделю, затем по готовности.
         Для этого нужны:
         - короткоживущие ветки и частое слияние в основную ветку;
         - флаги функций, чтобы незаконченный код уезжал в production выключенным;
         - миграции базы обратно совместимыми шагами (expand and contract), чтобы откат не требовал обратной
           миграции.

         Следующий шаг делать, только когда метрики стабильности на предыдущем не ухудшились.
      6. **Внедрять вместе с командой.** Показать данные на ретроспективе, договориться о цели и первом
         эксперименте, назначить владельцев конкретных шагов автоматизации. Заложить время на эту работу в
         планирование, а не оставлять её на "свободное время". Если сервисов несколько, начать с пилота на одном.
      7. **Договориться с бизнесом и измерять.** Менеджмент может считать, что частые релизы - это больше риска.
         Аргумент: маленький релиз проще проверить, диагностировать и откатить, а исследования DORA показывают, что
         скорость и стабильность улучшаются вместе, а не за счёт друг друга. Регулярно показывать тренд: частота
         растёт, доля хотфиксов и время восстановления падают. Если стабильность ухудшилась, замедлиться и укрепить
         автоматизацию, а не возвращаться к ежемесячным релизам.
    explanation: |
      Ключевая идея - частота снижает сложность. Мартин Фаулер формулирует её как "если больно, делайте это чаще".
      Сложность выпуска растёт быстрее, чем объём изменений в нём: чем больше изменений выкладывается вместе, тем
      больше между ними взаимодействий и тем дольше ищется причина сбоя. Частые релизы держат каждую партию
      маленькой и заставляют автоматизировать то, что при редких релизах терпят вручную.

      Ежемесячный релиз с ручным чек-листом - замкнутый круг: выкладка болезненная, поэтому её делают редко, партия
      растёт, и выкладка становится ещё болезненнее. Добавление пунктов в чек-лист после каждого хотфикса этот круг
      только усиливает.

      Метрики DORA подобраны парами: время выполнения изменений и частота развёртываний описывают скорость, доля
      неудачных изменений и время восстановления описывают стабильность. Если смотреть только на частоту, команда
      может начать выкладывать чаще ценой качества; если только на сбои, легко снова замедлиться. Метрики нужны
      команде для улучшения, а не для сравнения команд или наказания.

      На уровне лида ответ - это не только технический рецепт, но и порядок шагов: сначала снизить ущерб, затем
      автоматизировать, затем уменьшать партию, с договорённостью внутри команды, выделенным временем и понятными
      для бизнеса данными.
