  en:
    title: "A monthly Friday evening release almost always needs a hotfix: what do you change as tech lead?"
    prompt: |
      Your team releases a .NET service once a month, on Friday evening. Before the deployment a long manual
      checklist is followed. Even so, most releases are followed by an urgent hotfix. You are the tech lead.

      What do you change, in what order, and how do you know the changes work?
    hint: What grows together with the interval between releases, and how does that affect finding the cause when something breaks after a deployment?
    answer: |
      1. **Collect facts, not opinions.** For the last several releases find out:
         - how many changes (tasks, pull requests) went into each release;
         - how many hotfixes were needed and what caused each one;
         - which checklist steps take the most time and where mistakes happen most often.

         Record baseline values of the DORA metrics: change lead time (from commit to production), deployment
         frequency, change failure rate (here, the share of releases that needed a hotfix or a rollback) and the
         time to recover from a failed deployment.
      2. **Name the real cause.** The problem is not the people and not a lack of checks, it is the batch size. A
         month accumulates dozens of changes, they interact with each other, and when something breaks it is hard to
         tell which change is to blame. Feedback arrives weeks after the code was written. A long manual checklist is
         rarely followed the same way twice. Friday evening adds fatigue and a weekend without the people who know
         the changes.
      3. **Reduce the damage right away, without rebuilding anything.** Move the deployment to a morning in the
         middle of the working week, when the whole team is around. For every release decide up front who owns it and
         how it is rolled back. This does not cure the cause, but it lowers the cost of failures while the main work
         goes on.
      4. **Turn the checklist into a pipeline.** Every checklist step is a candidate for automation: building one
         artifact, tests, applying migrations, deployment, smoke tests after the deployment, rolling back to the
         previous artifact. Start with the steps where mistakes happen most often or that take the longest. Whatever
         cannot be automated yet stays as a short explicit list.
      5. **Shrink the batch step by step.** Move to a release every two weeks, then every week, then whenever a
         change is ready. This needs:
         - short-lived branches and frequent merges into the main branch;
         - feature flags, so that unfinished code goes to production switched off;
         - database migrations in backward-compatible steps (expand and contract), so that a rollback needs no
           reverse migration.

         Take the next step only when the stability metrics did not get worse on the previous one.
      6. **Roll it out with the team.** Show the data in a retrospective, agree on the goal and the first
         experiment, assign owners to concrete automation steps. Plan time for this work instead of leaving it to
         "spare time". If there are several services, start with a pilot on one.
      7. **Align with the business and measure.** Management may believe that frequent releases mean more risk. The
         argument: a small release is easier to check, diagnose and roll back, and DORA research shows that speed and
         stability improve together rather than at each other's expense. Show the trend regularly: frequency goes up,
         the hotfix share and recovery time go down. If stability gets worse, slow down and strengthen the automation
         instead of going back to monthly releases.
    explanation: |
      The key idea is that frequency reduces difficulty. Martin Fowler puts it as "if it hurts, do it more often".
      The difficulty of a release grows faster than the amount of change in it: the more changes ship together, the
      more interactions there are between them and the longer it takes to find the cause of a failure. Frequent
      releases keep each batch small and force you to automate what rare releases let you tolerate by hand.

      A monthly release with a manual checklist is a vicious circle: deploying is painful, so it is done rarely, the
      batch grows, and deploying becomes even more painful. Adding checklist items after every hotfix only makes the
      circle tighter.

      The DORA metrics come in pairs: change lead time and deployment frequency describe throughput, change failure
      rate and recovery time describe stability. Watching only frequency invites shipping faster at the cost of
      quality; watching only failures makes it easy to slow down again. The metrics are for the team to improve, not
      for comparing teams or punishing them.

      At lead level the answer is not only a technical recipe but also the order of steps: first reduce the damage,
      then automate, then shrink the batch, with agreement inside the team, dedicated time and data the business can
      understand.
    linkTitles:
      - "Martin Fowler: FrequencyReducesDifficulty"
      - "DORA's software delivery metrics: the four keys"

  en:
    title: "The on-call engineer gets about 200 alerts a week and missed a real outage: what do you do as tech lead?"
    prompt: |
      The on-call engineer of your team receives about 200 alerts a week. Most of them have not been looked at for a
      long time: people acknowledge and close them without reading. Last week the alert for a real outage got lost in
      this stream, and users reported the problem first. You are the tech lead.

      What do you do right away and what afterwards to make on-call work again? How do you roll the changes out in
      the team?
    hint: What must be true of an alert to justify waking someone up at 3 a.m.? And what happens to the alert stream in six months if nothing in the process changes?
    answer: |
      1. **Close the missed outage first.** Run a blameless postmortem: did an alert fire and get lost among others,
         was it muted or routed to the wrong place, or was there no alert for this symptom at all? Add an alert on
         the symptom of this failure right away (error rate or latency of the affected user flow, a synthetic check),
         so the gap does not stay open while the cleanup is under way.
      2. **Collect data before cutting.** Export the alert history for the last 4-8 weeks. For each rule: how many
         times it fired, whether anyone did anything in response, how long until it was acknowledged, whether it
         duplicates another alert, whether it resolves by itself (flapping). Usually a few rules produce most of the noise.
      3. **Run an alert review with the service owners.** A rule stays a page only if it signals something urgent,
         requires a human action, and users are affected now or will be soon (for example, a disk that fills up in a
         few hours). Every other rule gets one of these outcomes:
         - **delete** - nobody acts on it, it duplicates another alert, or it always resolves by itself;
         - **downgrade to a ticket or a dashboard** - the problem is real but can wait until working hours, or it is
           a cause signal such as CPU at 80% or one restarted pod;
         - **fix** - the signal is right, but the threshold is poor, the window is too short, there is no grouping
           or deduplication;
         - **automate** - the response is always the same steps, so a script should do them instead of a person.

         Every remaining page has an owner and a runbook.
      4. **Page on symptoms, diagnose with causes.** Pages are built on what users see: error rate, latency,
         availability of key flows, ideally against SLOs. Cause metrics (CPU, queue length, GC) stay on dashboards
         and help find the reason after a symptom page.
      5. **Make alert quality a recurring process.**
         - at every on-call handover, review every page: was it useful and what needs to change;
         - alert rules live in the repository and change through pull requests with code review; a new page needs an
           owner, a runbook and a justification;
         - track pages per shift, the share of pages that required action, and the number of incidents first
           reported by users rather than by alerts;
         - alert changes are part of the action items of every incident review.
      6. **Manage the risk and the team.** The main objection is the fear of deleting the one important alert. So
         downgrade to a ticket first and watch for a couple of weeks, and keep all rules in version control so any
         change can be reverted. Get time for the cleanup as planned work rather than out of on-call time, and agree
         on a target load per shift with management.
    explanation: |
      Alert fatigue is the predictable result of alerting on causes instead of symptoms. A person can react with
      urgency only a few times a day. When most pages are noise, ignoring them becomes a sensible habit, and a real
      page is ignored along with the rest. So more alerts do not mean better detection of outages: they make it
      worse. The Google SRE book puts it this way: every page should be urgent, require action and thought, and a
      page with a rote response should be automated.

      Cause-based alerts are both noisy and incomplete. High CPU often does not affect users at all, while a
      failure with an unforeseen cause triggers no cause alert. An alert on the symptom of a user flow catches the
      failure whatever caused it.

      At lead level the one-off cleanup is the easy part. Without owners, review of new rules and a regular look at
      what paged the on-call engineer, the noise comes back within a few months. The SRE book also treats on-call
      load as a limit to keep: if a shift has more incidents than people can handle properly, that is a problem to
      fix, not something to tolerate.
    linkTitles:
      - "Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems"
      - "Google SRE Book: Being On-Call"

           рискованнее, а причину сбоя труднее найти.

    title: "Management wants a weekly change advisory board to approve every release: what do you propose instead?"
    prompt: |
      After a recent incident, management wants every production deployment of your .NET services to be
      approved at a weekly change advisory board (CAB) meeting.

      As tech lead, how do you argue for a different change approval model, what do you propose instead, and
      how do you introduce it so that management keeps the control it needs?
    hint: "How much does the board know about a specific change compared with a reviewer from the team? And what happens to the size of releases if they can go out only once a week?"
    answer: |
      1. **Start from the goal, not the mechanism.** Management wants fewer failed changes, clear accountability
         and an audit trail. Sometimes a regulatory requirement for segregation of duties is added. Agree with
         these goals and on how to measure them: change failure rate, time to restore service, lead time for
         changes and deployment frequency. Then the discussion is about which mechanism reaches the goals better,
         not about trust in the team.
      2. **Arguments against a weekly CAB.**
         - DORA research: approval by an external body is associated with longer lead time for changes, less
           frequent deployments and slower recovery, but not with a lower change failure rate.
         - A weekly window accumulates changes: a release carries a week of work, so each deployment is riskier
           and the cause of a failure is harder to find.
         - The board sees a description of the change, not the code. With dozens of items per meeting, approval
           turns into a formality.
         - Fixes also wait for the board, or go through an emergency path that bypasses it. Either way time to
           restore suffers.
      3. **The proposal: control built into the delivery process.**
         - Review of every change in a pull request: a protected main branch and at least one approval from
           someone other than the author. This is segregation of duties, at the level where the reviewer
           understands the change.
         - Automated gates in the deployment pipeline: build, tests, static analysis, dependency vulnerability
           scanning, deployment to a pre-production environment with smoke tests. One artifact is promoted through
           the environments. A failed gate stops the release, and nobody can skip it silently.
         - Safe rollout and rollback: canary or progressive rollout with health checks, feature flags, a
           rehearsed rollback.
         - An audit trail produced automatically: for each deployment you can see who wrote and who approved the
           change, which pipeline run and which artifact version went to which environment, and the linked work
           item. Auditors get the data from the tools instead of meeting minutes.
         - Risk tiers: routine changes go through the pipeline only. Rare high-risk changes (destructive database
           migrations, changes to shared infrastructure or security settings) also get a review by the relevant
           experts as soon as the change is ready, not on a weekly schedule.
      4. **A different role for the board.** The board stops approving individual changes and oversees the
         process: trends of incidents and failed changes, the gate rules in the pipeline, sample audits of
         deployments. Its expertise is used where it scales.
      5. **Introduce it as an experiment.** A pilot on one or two services, the four metrics before and after, the
         other services stay under the CAB during the pilot, and management decides by the data. Name the
         preconditions honestly: if tests and monitoring are weak, the first investment goes there, otherwise
         automated gates are only an appearance of control.
    explanation: |
      A heavyweight external approval looks like control, but it acts far from the change. The approver has the
      least context, the decision arrives late, and the delay itself makes changes larger and riskier. DORA
      describes exactly this: external approvals slow delivery and do not lower the change failure rate, while
      teams that rely on review within the team and on a pipeline that rejects bad changes deliver better.

      The proposed model does not remove control, it moves it: earlier (review before merge), to the people who
      understand the change, and into automation that runs on every change and cannot be forgotten. Continuous
      delivery rests on the same idea: the pipeline keeps every change in a releasable state, so the decision to
      deploy becomes low risk.

      The lead's task here is less technical than persuasive: accept management's goals, offer measurable
      criteria, a reversible pilot and a meaningful role for the board instead of fighting it. A weak answer is
      just "the CAB is bad, remove it" without an audit trail, risk tiers and a transition plan.

      - "DORA: Streamlining change approval"
      - "Martin Fowler: Continuous Delivery"

  en:
    title: How do you roll out code and configuration changes to a platform in dozens of regions so that one bad change cannot cause a global outage?
    prompt: |
      A .NET platform runs in several dozen cloud regions. Every day it receives changes to code, configuration,
      feature flags and infrastructure. Management requires that a single bad change must never be able to take
      down all regions at once.

      How do you design the rollout process? Which stages does it go through, what decides whether it may
      proceed, how does rollback work, which changes does it cover, and what do you pay for this design?
    hint: How many regions should see a change before you get the first reliable signal about its quality? And how does a configuration change differ from a code change in terms of risk?
    answer: |
      1. **Progressive exposure in rings.** Every change goes through the same rings, each larger than the
         previous one:
         - ring 0: internal and test environments, company employees (dogfooding);
         - ring 1: one small region or one cell (scale unit) with little traffic - the canary;
         - ring 2: one region in each geography, but never both regions of a pair that disaster recovery
           relies on;
         - ring 3 and beyond: the remaining regions in waves of growing size.

         Inside a region the change also moves gradually: by availability zone, cell or share of instances,
         not to the whole region at once.
      2. **Bake time.** After each ring the change runs under real traffic for a while before it moves on.
         Early rings bake shorter, later rings longer, and the bake should cover peak hours. This catches
         problems that do not show up immediately: memory leaks, expiring caches and tokens, growing queues.
      3. **Automated health gates.** Moving to the next ring is approved not by a person's gut feeling but by a
         check: error rate, latency and business metrics (successful orders, sign-ins) of the new version are
         compared with a baseline or with neighbouring cells on the old version. If they are worse than a
         threshold, the pipeline **halts the rollout by itself** and starts the rollback. This needs metrics and
         logs tagged with version and ring.
      4. **A fast, rehearsed rollback.** Rollback is a pipeline action practised in advance, not a manual
         procedure: restore the previous artifact, the previous configuration revision, switch the flag off. For
         it to be possible, versions N and N-1 must run side by side: API and message contracts are compatible
         in both directions, and the database schema changes with expand and contract.
      5. **Configuration is a change too.** Configuration, feature flags, routing rules, certificates, WAF rules
         and network policies go through the same rings and the same gates as code, live in a repository and
         are versioned. Pushing configuration instantly and globally, bypassing the rings, is a typical path to
         a global outage.
      6. **No global single points.** Rings bound the blast radius only when regions are independent. A global
         control plane, a shared configuration store or shared DNS needs its own staged rollout, and regions
         must keep running on the last known good configuration when the global component is unavailable
         (static stability).
      7. **Process discipline.**
         - One rollout of one service at a time, so that when something degrades it is clear which change is
           to blame.
         - Urgent fixes also go through the rings, only with a shorter bake. Skipping the rings entirely is a
           break-glass procedure with explicit approval and an audit record.
         - During an incident, rollouts to the remaining regions are frozen.
      8. **The cost.**
         - A full rollout takes days, not minutes, and a fix also reaches all regions with a delay.
         - Several versions run in production at the same time, hence the compatibility requirements.
         - You need a pipeline that manages rings, per-version metrics and baseline comparison.
         - The signal from a small ring can be statistically weak, and rare or region-specific defects may
           only show up in late rings.
    explanation: |
      The goal of the design is a bounded blast radius: at any moment a defective change can affect only the
      part of the system that has already received it. If a change goes to every region at once, no amount of
      regional redundancy helps: all copies break the same way at the same time. Rings turn a global risk into a
      sequence of local ones, where each next step is taken only after evidence that the previous one is healthy.

      Automated gates matter because people are slow and inconsistent, especially at night: while the on-call
      engineer is reading a dashboard, the pipeline could already have stopped itself. Bake time matters because
      many defects are invisible in the first minutes.

      Configuration deserves special attention. Its changes look harmless and often propagate instantly, which is
      why many large cloud outages are caused by them. A strong answer explicitly puts configuration, flags,
      certificates and infrastructure rules through the same rings.

      The trade-off is direct: release speed in exchange for bounded damage. For a platform where a global outage
      costs more than a release delayed by a few days, it is a good deal, but it requires investment in
      observability, version compatibility and regional independence.
    linkTitles:
      - "Azure Well-Architected Framework: safe deployment practices"
      - "Google SRE Workbook: Canarying Releases"

    title: First on-call shift, a night page for an alert in a service you do not know. What do you do?
    prompt: |
      You are a middle developer on your first on-call shift. At 3 a.m. you are paged for an alert in a service
      owned by another part of the team, whose code you have never worked with. What do you do, and in what
      order?
    hint: Is your job on call to fix any failure yourself, or to make sure the people who can solve it are working on it quickly?
    answer: |
      1. **Acknowledge the page within the agreed time.** The team and the paging system need to see that the
         page is taken and someone is already looking at the problem.
      2. **Assess the impact in a few minutes.** Read the alert text and open the dashboard linked to it: are
         users affected, is the problem growing or already over, were there recent deploys or configuration
         changes. That sets the urgency.
      3. **Open the runbook.** Find the response instructions the alert links to or that live in the service
         documentation, and perform only the safe steps described there. Do not improvise in an unfamiliar
         system: a random restart, data deletion or configuration change can turn a small failure into a big one.
      4. **Escalate early, along the agreed path.** If there is no runbook, it does not help, or user impact is
         serious, call the next person in the chain at once: the secondary on-call, the on-call of the team that
         owns the service, the incident commander. Set yourself a time box up front, for example 15-20 minutes
         without clear progress. If users are affected, declare an incident following the team's procedure.
         Waking a colleague is cheaper than an extra hour of outage.
      5. **Keep notes and report status.** In the incident channel, briefly write what you see, what you did and
         when. Whoever joins does not have to ask again, and the notes become the timeline for the review.
      6. **Follow through after the shift.** Hand the context over to the next on-call and file tasks for the
         gaps you found: a missing or outdated runbook, an unclear or useless alert, missing access. If there
         was an incident, take part in a blameless postmortem.
    explanation: |
      The on-call engineer is not responsible for fixing any service single-handedly, but for getting the
      problem worked on quickly and keeping the damage small. The Google SRE book chapter on being on call names
      the resources that make on-call less daunting: clear escalation paths, well-defined incident management
      procedures and a blameless postmortem culture. Escalating along such a path is a normal part of the
      process, not an admission of weakness.

      The same chapter notes that under stress people tend to act intuitively and hastily instead of
      deliberately. In an unfamiliar system intuition is at its weakest, so a runbook and an early call to
      someone who knows the service are more reliable than trying to understand the code at night. The chapter
      on managing incidents adds that it is better to declare an incident early and close it after a simple fix
      than to start the procedure hours later, when the problem has grown.

      Weak answers: leaving the alert until morning, silently restarting everything, spending an hour in someone
      else's code because you are embarrassed to wake anyone. If a newcomer does not know the escalation path or
      lacks access, that is a team gap worth closing before the first shift, for example by shadowing an
      experienced colleague on call.

  en:
    title: The team's estimates are consistently half the real time. How do you improve forecasts?
    prompt: |
      For several months the team's tasks have taken about twice as long as estimated, and release date
      forecasts are regularly missed. As a senior developer, how would you propose to improve the forecasts? Why
      is simply asking everyone to "estimate with a buffer" a poor solution?
    hint: If the error is always about the same size, where should the correction live - in each new guess or in how estimates are turned into dates?
    answer: |
      - **Understand the error first.** A consistent underestimate of about two times is rather good news: the
        error is systematic, so it can be calibrated. Check whether it is the same for different kinds of tasks
        and where the gap comes from: unplanned work (support, incidents, urgent bugs), a definition of done
        that leaves out review, tests and deployment, scope growing during the work, waiting for other teams.
      - **Do not add a buffer to every new estimate.** If everyone inflates their own guess "just in case", the
        buffer differs between people, is hidden and cannot be checked, and after the next miss it gets tweaked
        blindly again.
      - **Calibrate the forecast on measured data.** Keep estimates relative (story points or ideal days) and
        turn them into calendar dates through the team's measured velocity: the amount of estimated work that
        is actually finished per iteration. An alternative without point estimates is throughput (how many items
        are closed per week) and cycle time. Plan the next iteration by what was done in recent iterations, not
        by available hours.
      - **Forecast as a range.** Divide the remaining work by the lowest and highest velocity of the last few
        iterations and recompute the forecast as data comes in.
      - **Improve the estimates themselves.** Split work into smaller items, include review, tests and
        deployment in the definition of done, account for the share of unplanned work, and compare a new task
        with similar finished ones.
      - **Do not make velocity a target.** Do not compare teams by it, do not demand that it grows and do not
        judge people by it. Otherwise estimates get inflated and the calibration stops working.
      - **Remember why you estimate.** Precision is needed for a specific decision: sometimes a rough forecast
        is enough and refining it is not worth the time.
    explanation: |
      People systematically underestimate their own work, and persuasion barely fixes that. A stable bias,
      however, is easy to correct with data. Martin Fowler describes velocity as the amount of estimated work
      finished per iteration: the estimate units do not have to match calendar time, because velocity converts
      them into dates. If a team is consistently twice as optimistic, its velocity simply comes out at half the
      "expected" value, and a forecast built on it is correct. The correction lives in one measured number, not
      in each estimator's head.

      A buffer on every estimate treats the symptom: it is not based on data, differs between people and hides
      the real causes of the gap, such as constant unplanned work or an incomplete definition of done.
      Measuring, on the contrary, makes them visible.

      Fowler also warns that velocity is a planning tool, not a measure of productivity. Once it becomes a
      target, the team starts inflating estimates, the number grows without more real work, and the forecasting
      tool breaks. Finally, an estimate is valuable only when it helps make a decision, so the effort spent on
      its precision should match how important that decision is.
    linkTitles:
      - "XP Velocity (Martin Fowler)"
      - "Purpose of Estimation (Martin Fowler)"

         конфликтам, а в одном случае изменилось поведение при ошибке»), затем спросить о причинах: не нравится
         подход, код не соответствует соглашениям команды, не хотелось спорить на ревью.
      3. **Просить о коммуникации, а не о запрете.** Код общий, и коллега вправе его менять. Договориться о
         другом: если правка существенно меняет недавно влитый код, добавить автора в ревьюеры или хотя бы
         написать ему; замечания к подходу высказывать на ревью до слияния, а не переписывать код после.
      4. **Превратить договорённость в норму команды.** Поднять тему на ретроспективе как общий вопрос, без
         указания на человека: как мы рефакторим чужой свежий код и как об этом сообщаем. Спорные вопросы стиля
         закрепить в `.editorconfig`, правилах анализаторов или документе с соглашениями, чтобы их не решали
         молчаливым переписыванием.
      5. **Не начинать с отката или эскалации.** Не откатывать его правки и не переписывать код обратно - это
         война правок. К тимлиду идти, только если после разговора и договорённости ничего не меняется и это
         мешает работе команды.
    explanation: |
      Мартин Фаулер описывает три модели владения кодом. При строгом владении модуль закреплён за одним
      человеком, и менять его может только он. При слабом у модуля есть владелец, но другие разработчики тоже
      могут менять его код, а существенные изменения принято сначала обсудить с владельцем. При коллективном
      владении код принадлежит команде, и любой может менять любую его часть. Если в команде принято слабое или
      коллективное владение, претензия «он трогает мой код» неверна по сути: это код команды. Сильный ответ это
      признаёт.

      Проблема в другом - в отсутствии коммуникации. Автор узнаёт о правках по конфликтам слияния, знание о том,
      почему код изменился, теряется, а несогласие по дизайну не высказывается открыто и решается молчаливым
      переписыванием. Именно это и нужно обсуждать.

      Порядок действий важен. Разговор наедине с конкретными примерами даёт коллеге шанс объясниться и не ставит
      его в неловкое положение перед командой. Откат его правок превращает разногласие в войну правок, а жалоба
      руководителю до прямого разговора подрывает доверие и лишает вас возможности решить вопрос самим. Командная
      норма переводит личный конфликт в процесс: правило действует для всех и снимает ощущение, что кто-то
      кого-то контролирует.

      Слабые ответы: молча терпеть и копить раздражение, требовать «не трогать мой код», откатывать правки,
      сразу идти к руководителю.

      - "Владение кодом (Мартин Фаулер)"
  en:
    title: A teammate keeps rewriting code you merged without telling you. How do you handle it?
    prompt: |
      Over the last month a teammate has three times rewritten parts of code that you recently merged into the
      main branch. They renamed classes, restructured a service and changed the error handling. Each time it
      happened in their own pull requests, and you were neither added as a reviewer nor told. You find out when
      your next task runs into merge conflicts or when the code behaves differently from what you remember.
      What do you do?
    hint: |
      Who owns the code in a team, and what actually gets in the way of the work - the changes themselves, or the way you learn about them?
    answer: |
      1. **Sort out the facts and your own reaction.** Collect concrete examples: links to the PRs, what exactly
         changed and what it led to (conflicts, unexpected behaviour, lost time). Judge the changes honestly:
         some of them may really have improved the code or fixed something the review missed.
      2. **Talk in private.** Not in PR comments and not in the team chat. Describe the examples and their effect
         on the work without judging the person ("three PRs changed code I had just merged, I learned about it
         from conflicts, and in one case the error behaviour changed"), then ask about the reasons: they dislike
         the approach, the code does not follow team conventions, they did not want to argue in review.
      3. **Ask for communication, not for a ban.** The code is shared, and the teammate is entitled to change it.
         Agree on something else: if a change substantially reworks recently merged code, add the author as a
         reviewer or at least message them; raise objections to the approach in review before the merge instead
         of rewriting the code afterwards.
      4. **Turn the agreement into a team norm.** Raise the topic in a retrospective as a general question, without
         pointing at the person: how do we refactor someone else's fresh code and how do we announce it. Settle
         disputed style questions in `.editorconfig`, analyzer rules or a conventions document so that they are
         not decided by silent rewriting.
      5. **Do not start with a revert or an escalation.** Do not revert their changes or rewrite the code back -
         that is an edit war. Go to the team lead only if nothing changes after the conversation and the agreement
         and it hurts the team's work.
    explanation: |
      Martin Fowler describes three models of code ownership. With strong ownership a module belongs to one
      person and only they may change it. With weak ownership a module has an owner, but other developers may
      change its code too, and it is expected to talk a substantial change over with the owner first. With
      collective ownership the code belongs to the team and anyone may change any part of it. If the team uses
      weak or collective ownership, the complaint "they touch my code" is wrong in substance: it is the team's
      code. A strong answer acknowledges that.

      The problem is something else - the missing communication. The author learns about the changes from merge
      conflicts, the knowledge of why the code changed is lost, and a design disagreement is not voiced openly but
      settled by silent rewriting. That is what needs to be discussed.

      The order matters. A private conversation with concrete examples gives the teammate a chance to explain and
      does not embarrass them in front of the team. Reverting their changes turns a disagreement into an edit war,
      and complaining to the manager before talking directly damages trust and takes away your chance to solve it
      yourselves. A team norm turns a personal conflict into a process: the rule applies to everyone and removes
      the feeling that someone is policing someone else.

      Weak answers: putting up with it silently while the irritation builds, demanding "do not touch my code",
      reverting the changes, going straight to the manager.
    linkTitles:
      - "Code Ownership (Martin Fowler)"

    title: Как senior-разработчику выстроить первые недели нового члена команды, чтобы тот быстро стал продуктивным?

      В вашу команду приходит новый разработчик, и вам поручили ввести его в работу. Как вы выстроите его
      первые недели и почему именно так? Какой подход к вводу в команду, по-вашему, работает хуже всего?
    hint: |
      Что новичок узнаёт, когда сам проводит небольшое изменение через весь путь до production, и чего он не узнает из документации?
    answer: |
      - **Подготовить всё до первого дня.** Доступы, рабочее окружение, которое поднимается по инструкции или
        скрипту, назначенный наставник-напарник (buddy) с выделенным временем и заранее отобранные небольшие
        реальные задачи.
      - **Первые дни - контекст и рабочее окружение.** Короткий обзор продукта, схемы архитектуры и того, кто за
        что отвечает. Новичок собирает решение и запускает тесты у себя; всё, что в инструкции устарело, он сам
        исправляет - это первый полезный вклад.
      - **В первую неделю выпустить небольшое реальное изменение.** Исправление ошибки или маленькое улучшение,
        сделанное в паре с напарником и прошедшее весь обычный путь: ветка, тесты, PR, ревью, CI, деплой, проверка
        в мониторинге. Изменение должно быть маленьким, чтобы ревью было быстрым.
      - **Дальше - парная работа над задачами из бэклога.** Новичок чаще за клавиатурой, напарник подсказывает
        направление. Партнёров по паре стоит менять, чтобы новичок познакомился с командой и разными частями
        системы. Постепенно - самостоятельные задачи с регулярными сверками, ревью чужих PR, позже дежурство
        в роли наблюдателя рядом с опытным коллегой.
      - **Явные ожидания и обратная связь.** Договориться, что значит «освоился» к концу первого месяца, проводить
        регулярные встречи один на один и спрашивать новичка, что в процессе ввода мешало, чтобы улучшить его
        для следующих.

    explanation: |
      Работающая модель системы складывается из практики, а не из чтения. Многое из того, что нужно знать в
      команде, нигде не записано: почему код устроен именно так, к кому идти с вопросом, как на самом деле
      проходит релиз. Это знание передаётся в совместной работе. Документация к тому же быстро устаревает, и
      новичок не может отличить актуальное от устаревшего.

      Раннее реальное изменение решает сразу несколько задач. Новичок проходит весь конвейер поставки и
      натыкается на пробелы в доступах и инструкциях в первую неделю, а не через месяц. Он получает быструю
      обратную связь на ревью и уверенность, что его работа попадает к пользователям. Руководство Google по
      code review объясняет, почему изменение должно быть небольшим: маленькие изменения ревьюят быстрее и
      тщательнее, и их проще влить.

      Статья о парном программировании на сайте Мартина Фаулера называет передачу знаний и ввод новых людей в
      команду среди главных пользы парной работы. Она же предупреждает, что работа в паре утомляет, поэтому

  en:
    title: How should a senior developer structure a new team member's first weeks so they become productive quickly?
    prompt: |
      A new developer joins your team, and you are asked to onboard them. How do you structure their first
      weeks, and why that way? Which approach to onboarding do you think works worst?
    hint: |
      What does a newcomer learn by taking a small change all the way to production themselves, and what will they never learn from the documentation?
    answer: |
      - **Prepare everything before day one.** Access, a development environment that comes up from instructions
        or a script, a named buddy with time set aside, and a few small real tasks picked in advance.
      - **First days - context and the environment.** A short overview of the product, an architecture map and
        who is responsible for what. The newcomer builds the solution and runs the tests locally; whatever is
        stale in the setup instructions they fix themselves - their first useful contribution.
      - **Ship a small real change in the first week.** A bug fix or a small improvement, done in a pair with the
        buddy and taken through the whole normal path: branch, tests, PR, review, CI, deploy, a check in
        monitoring. The change should be small so that the review is quick.
      - **Then pair on backlog tasks.** The newcomer is at the keyboard most of the time and the buddy suggests
        the direction. Rotate pairing partners so the newcomer meets the team and different parts of the system.
        Gradually move to solo tasks with regular check-ins, reviewing other people's PRs, and later shadowing an
        experienced colleague on call.
      - **Explicit expectations and feedback.** Agree on what "settled in" means by the end of the first month,
        hold regular one-on-ones, and ask the newcomer what got in the way during onboarding so it improves for
        the next person.
      - **What works worst** is "here is the wiki, read it for a couple of weeks": the newcomer reads partly
        stale documentation alone, does not apply what they read and gets no feedback.
    explanation: |
      A working mental model of a system comes from practice, not from reading. Much of what a team needs to know
      is written down nowhere: why the code is shaped the way it is, whom to ask about what, how a release really
      happens. That knowledge passes on through working together. Documentation also goes stale quickly, and a
      newcomer cannot tell what is current and what is not.

      An early real change solves several problems at once. The newcomer walks the whole delivery pipeline and
      runs into gaps in access and instructions in the first week rather than a month later. They get fast
      feedback in review and the confidence that their work reaches users. Google's code review guide explains
      why the change should be small: small changes are reviewed more quickly and more thoroughly, and they are
      easier to merge.

      The article on pair programming on Martin Fowler's site names knowledge sharing and onboarding new people
      among the main benefits of pairing. It also warns that pairing is exhausting, so pairing all day for a long
      period is a bad idea: alternate it with solo work. When an experienced person pairs with a newcomer, the
      experienced one should give the newcomer time to figure things out instead of dictating every line.

      A named buddy matters because a newcomer hesitates to interrupt "everyone": they need one specific person
      they can ask anything, and that person needs time for it.
    linkTitles:
      - "On Pair Programming (martinfowler.com)"
      - "Small CLs (Google Engineering Practices)"

      2. **Собрать факты обеих сторон в одну хронологию.** История деплоев и изменений конфигурации обоих
         сервисов, какую версию API или схемы использовала каждая сторона, логи и трассировки упавших вызовов с
         реальными примерами запросов и ответов, алерты и момент, когда каждая команда заметила проблему. Это один
         общий документ, который обе команды могут дополнять и комментировать, а не две версии событий.
      3. **Провести одну совместную встречу без поиска виноватых.** Участвуют обе команды. Ведущий не должен
         принадлежать ни одной из них: раз вы сами из команды заказов, попросите инженера или лида из третьей
         команды, или хотя бы открыто признайте свою заинтересованность. Правила: говорим о событиях и системах,
         а не о людях и командах; сначала согласуем хронологию, и только потом обсуждаем причины.
      4. **Заменить вопрос.** Вместо «кто нарушил контракт» спросить «где этот контракт записан и что его
         проверяет». Обычно оказывается, что контракт существовал только неявно: поставщик внёс изменение, которое
         считал совместимым (например, новое обязательное поле или новое значение перечисления), потребитель
         опирался на поведение, которое нигде не описано, ни один тест ни с одной стороны не ловил расхождение, а об
         изменении никто не объявил. Причины есть с обеих сторон и в промежутке между ними.
      5. **Закончить общими задачами по интерфейсу.** Явный версионируемый контракт (например, описание OpenAPI
         там, где его видят обе команды), контрактные тесты от потребителя, которые запускаются в CI поставщика,
         правило обратно совместимых изменений и вывода из употребления с заранее объявленным сроком, терпимый к
         лишним полям разбор ответов на стороне потребителя, метрики и алерты на ошибки интеграции, видимые обеим
         командам, и канал для объявления изменений. У каждой задачи есть владелец и срок; ключевые задачи
         принадлежат обеим командам вместе.
      6. **Довести до конца.** Опубликовать один общий постмортем, отслеживать выполнение задач и отдельно,
         наедине, поговорить с лидами обеих команд о тоне в чате - это не тема для документа. Эскалировать
         руководству стоит только если команды не могут договориться о задачах.
    explanation: |
      Вопрос «кто виноват» в сбое интеграции почти никогда не имеет полезного ответа. Каждая команда видит только
      свою половину: свой код, свои деплои, свою трактовку контракта. Пока они спорят в чате, каждая собирает
      аргументы в свою пользу, позиции твердеют, и даже если «победитель» найден, следующий сбой на той же границе
      никто не предотвратил. Общая хронология из фактов обеих сторон заменяет спор о мнениях проверяемой картиной.

      Книга Google SRE описывает постмортем без поиска виноватых как разбор, который ищет причины, способствовавшие
      инциденту, не обвиняя ни отдельного человека, ни команду, и исходит из того, что все действовали с добрыми
      намерениями на основе той информации, что у них была. Там же объясняется, почему это важно: если за ошибку
      наказывают, люди перестают открыто рассказывать о проблемах. Для двух команд это особенно заметно: команда,
      которая ждёт обвинений, приносит на встречу защиту, а не логи.

      Сбои интеграции живут на границе, поэтому и исправлять нужно границу. Контракты, которые формулирует
      потребитель и проверяет поставщик (consumer-driven contracts), делают ожидания потребителя явными и
      показывают несовместимое изменение в CI поставщика, а не в production. Совместное владение такими задачами
      превращает две конфликтующие команды в участников общего решения.

      Слабые ответы: выступить судьёй и выбрать правую сторону, сразу эскалировать руководству, позволить каждой
      команде написать свой постмортем или ограничиться правкой одного поля, из-за которого упали вызовы.
    linkTitles:
      - "Культура постмортемов: учимся на ошибках (книга Google SRE)"
      - "Контракты, управляемые потребителем (Ian Robinson, сайт Мартина Фаулера)"
  en:
    title: After an integration outage two teams blame each other in chat for breaking the contract. How do you mediate?
    prompt: |
      At night checkout stopped working for two hours: your team's order service was getting errors from a
      neighbouring team's payment service. The service is restored, but the teams now blame each other in a shared
      chat. The payment team says you send requests that do not follow the contract, your colleagues say the payment
      team changed the API without notice. The messages get sharper, and managers join the argument.

      You are a senior developer on the order service team, and you have been asked to sort it out. What do you do,
      and in what order?
    hint: Will the answer to "whose fault is it" prevent the next such outage? Where is the contract between the teams actually written down, and what checks it?
    answer: |
      1. **Take the argument out of the chat.** Post one calm message in the channel: the service is restored, the
         analysis will be joint, at a set time, and until then we collect facts, not verdicts. Do not answer each
         accusation and do not defend your own team in public. Separately make sure the recovery is stable and the
         failure will not come back in the next few hours.
      2. **Gather both sides' facts into one timeline.** The deploy and configuration history of both services,
         which API or schema version each side used, logs and traces of the failing calls with real request and
         response examples, the alerts and the moment each team noticed the problem. This is one shared document
         that both teams can add to and comment on, not two versions of events.
      3. **Run one joint blameless session.** Both teams take part. The facilitator should belong to neither: since
         you are on the order team yourself, ask an engineer or lead from a third team, or at least state your own
         interest openly. Ground rules: talk about events and systems, not people and teams; agree on the timeline
         first, and only then discuss causes.
      4. **Change the question.** Instead of "who broke the contract" ask "where is this contract written down and
         what checks it". Usually it turns out that the contract existed only implicitly: the provider made a change
         it believed compatible (for example, a new required field or a new enum value), the consumer relied on
         behaviour that was documented nowhere, no test on either side caught the mismatch, and nobody announced the
         change. The causes sit on both sides and in the gap between them.
      5. **End with jointly owned actions for the interface.** An explicit, versioned contract (for example, an
         OpenAPI description where both teams can see it), consumer-driven contract tests that run in the provider's
         CI, a rule for backward-compatible changes and for deprecation with an announced date, response parsing on
         the consumer side that tolerates extra fields, metrics and alerts on integration errors visible to both
         teams, and a channel for announcing changes. Each item has an owner and a deadline; the key items belong to
         both teams together.
      6. **Close the loop.** Publish one joint postmortem, track the action items, and separately, in private,
         talk to both team leads about the tone in the chat - that is not a topic for the document. Escalate to
         management only if the teams cannot agree on the action items.
    explanation: |
      The question "whose fault is it" almost never has a useful answer in an integration outage. Each team sees
      only its half: its code, its deploys, its reading of the contract. While they argue in chat, each collects
      arguments for its own side, positions harden, and even if a "winner" is found, nobody has prevented the next
      failure at the same boundary. A shared timeline built from both sides' facts replaces a dispute of opinions
      with a picture that can be checked.

      The Google SRE book describes a blameless postmortem as an analysis that looks for the contributing causes of
      an incident without indicting any individual or team, and that assumes everyone acted with good intentions on
      the information they had. It also explains why this matters: if mistakes are punished, people stop bringing
      problems to light. Between two teams this is especially visible: a team that expects blame brings a defence to
      the meeting, not its logs.

      Integration failures live at the boundary, so the boundary is what needs fixing. Contracts that the consumer
      states and the provider verifies (consumer-driven contracts) make the consumer's expectations explicit and
      reveal an incompatible change in the provider's CI instead of in production. Joint ownership of these items
      turns two conflicting teams into participants in one shared fix.

      Weak answers: acting as a judge and picking the side that is right, escalating to management at once, letting
      each team write its own postmortem, or stopping at fixing the one field that made the calls fail.
    linkTitles:
      - "Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure (Google SRE book)"
      - "Consumer-Driven Contracts: A Service Evolution Pattern (Ian Robinson, martinfowler.com)"

  ru:
    title: Как техлиду сократить время выполнения задач, если у каждого разработчика в работе три-четыре задачи одновременно?
    prompt: |
      Вы техлид. Задачи команды выполняются неделями, хотя каждая по отдельности требует нескольких дней работы.
      На доске видно, что у каждого разработчика в работе три-четыре задачи: одна ждёт code review, другая
      заблокирована ответом соседней команды, третью начали вчера. Все загружены, но до конца доходит мало.
      Что вы предложите команде, как это обоснуете и как ответите тем, кто опасается, что разработчики
      начнут простаивать?
    hint: Если число людей не меняется, а начатых задач становится больше, что происходит со временем, которое каждая задача проводит в работе?
    answer: |
      - **Сделать поток видимым и измеримым.** Описать на доске реальные этапы работы (разработка, review,
        тестирование, ожидание внешней команды) и начать отслеживать метрики потока: количество задач в работе
        (WIP), время выполнения (cycle time - от начала работы над задачей до её завершения), возраст начатых
        задач и пропускную способность. Обычно выясняется, что большую часть времени задачи не делаются,
        а ждут: review, ответа, освободившегося человека.
      - **Объяснить связь WIP и времени выполнения.** По закону Литтла среднее время выполнения равно среднему
        WIP, делённому на среднюю пропускную способность. Если пропускная способность команды не растёт, каждая
        лишняя начатая задача удлиняет путь всех остальных. Вдобавок переключение между задачами стоит времени
        и внимания, а частично сделанная работа не приносит ценности, пока не завершена.
      - **Договориться о явных лимитах WIP вместе с командой.** Лимит устанавливает команда, а не техлид
        единолично. Начать с лимита ниже текущего уровня (например, на команду или на этап review), записать
        его на доске и соблюдать как правило. Новая задача берётся (pull) только тогда, когда освободилось место.
      - **«Меньше начинать, больше заканчивать».** Упёрлись в лимит - не начинать новое, а помогать довести
        начатое: сделать review, поработать в паре, снять блокировку. Приоритет у задач, которые ближе к концу
        или дольше всех находятся в работе.
      - **Убрать причины, по которым задачи копятся.** Блокировки от внешних команд эскалировать и обсуждать
        как системную проблему, review сделать приоритетом команды, а не делом «когда будет время». С владельцем
        продукта договориться о порядке поступления работы, срочные задачи ограничить отдельным небольшим лимитом.
      - **Ответить на страх простоя.** Загрузка каждого человека - не цель: цель - быстрее и предсказуемее
        доводить работу до пользователя. Разработчик без своей новой задачи помогает завершать чужие, и это
        полезная работа. Показывать руководству тренд времени выполнения и пропускной способности, а не
        процент занятости.
      - **Проверять и подстраивать.** Пересматривать лимиты на ретроспективах по данным: если задачи всё ещё
        долго ждут, лимит можно снизить; если работа систематически простаивает из-за нехватки задач на каком-то
        этапе, его корректируют. Сформулировать ожидаемый уровень сервиса (например, «85% задач завершаются за
        N дней») и сверяться с ним.
    explanation: |
      Когда у каждого по три-четыре задачи, команда выглядит максимально загруженной, но эта загрузка во многом
      состоит из ожидания и переключений. Время выполнения задачи складывается не только из работы над ней, но
      и из времени в очередях: пока задача ждёт review или ответа, её автор начинает следующую, и очередь
      растёт. Закон Литтла связывает три величины потока: при той же пропускной способности больше WIP означает
      больше среднее время выполнения. Поэтому сократить время выполнения можно, не ускоряя людей, а уменьшая
      количество одновременно начатой работы.

      Kanban Guide описывает эту идею как явный контроль WIP: команда ограничивает количество начатых задач,
      что создаёт систему вытягивания (pull), где новая работа начинается только при освобождении мощности.
      Там же определены метрики, на которые стоит опираться: WIP, пропускная способность, возраст задачи и время
      выполнения, а также ожидаемый уровень сервиса как прогноз времени выполнения.

      Главное сопротивление обычно не техническое, а психологическое: руководители и сами разработчики привыкли
      оценивать работу по занятости. Сильный техлид не вводит лимиты приказом, а договаривается о них с командой
      как об эксперименте, показывает данные до и после и защищает команду от давления «начать ещё одно». Слабые
      ответы: требовать работать быстрее, добавлять людей, просто запрещать брать новые задачи без работы
      с причинами блокировок или устанавливать лимит, который никто не соблюдает.
    linkTitles:
      - "Kanban Guide (kanbanguides.org)"
      - "Kanban Guide для Scrum-команд (scrum.org)"
  en:
    title: How does a tech lead shorten cycle time when every developer has three or four tasks in progress at once?
    prompt: |
      You are a tech lead. The team's tasks take weeks to finish, even though each one needs only a few days of
      work. The board shows that every developer has three or four tasks in progress: one waits for code review,
      another is blocked on a reply from a neighbouring team, the third was started yesterday. Everyone is busy,
      but little gets finished. What do you propose to the team, how do you justify it, and what do you tell
      people who worry that developers will end up idle?
    hint: If the number of people stays the same but the number of started tasks grows, what happens to the time each task spends in progress?
    answer: |
      - **Make the flow visible and measurable.** Model the real stages of work on the board (development,
        review, testing, waiting for another team) and start tracking flow metrics: work in progress (WIP),
        cycle time (from the start of work on an item until it is finished), the age of started items and
        throughput. It usually turns out that most of the time items are not being worked on but waiting: for
        review, for a reply, for a free person.
      - **Explain the link between WIP and cycle time.** By Little's Law, average cycle time equals average WIP
        divided by average throughput. If the team's throughput does not grow, every extra started task makes
        all the others take longer. On top of that, switching between tasks costs time and attention, and
        partially done work delivers no value until it is finished.
      - **Agree on explicit WIP limits with the team.** The team sets the limit, not the lead alone. Start with
        a limit below the current level (for example, per team or for the review stage), write it on the board
        and follow it as a rule. A new item is pulled only when a slot frees up.
      - **"Stop starting, start finishing".** When the limit is reached, do not start something new; help finish
        what is started: do a review, pair, remove a blocker. Items closest to done or oldest in progress come
        first.
      - **Remove the reasons work piles up.** Escalate blockers from other teams and treat them as a systemic
        problem, make review a team priority rather than something done "when there is time". Agree with the
        product owner on how work enters the team, and give urgent items their own small limit.
      - **Answer the fear of idleness.** Keeping every person busy is not the goal: the goal is to deliver work
        to users faster and more predictably. A developer without a new task of their own helps finish others'
        tasks, and that is useful work. Show management the trend of cycle time and throughput, not the
        percentage of busy people.
      - **Inspect and adapt.** Review the limits in retrospectives using the data: if items still wait for a
        long time, the limit can go lower; if a stage regularly starves for work, adjust it. Define a service
        level expectation (for example, "85% of items finish within N days") and check against it.
    explanation: |
      When everyone has three or four tasks, the team looks fully utilised, but much of that utilisation is
      waiting and switching. An item's cycle time is not only the time spent working on it but also the time
      spent in queues: while an item waits for review or a reply, its author starts the next one, and the queue
      grows. Little's Law connects three flow quantities: with the same throughput, more WIP means a longer
      average cycle time. So cycle time can be cut without making people faster, by reducing the amount of work
      started at the same time.

      The Kanban Guide describes this idea as explicitly controlling WIP: the team limits the number of started
      items, which creates a pull system where new work starts only when capacity frees up. It also defines the
      metrics to rely on: WIP, throughput, work item age and cycle time, plus a service level expectation as a
      forecast of cycle time.

      The main resistance is usually psychological rather than technical: managers and developers themselves
      are used to judging work by how busy people are. A strong lead does not impose limits by decree but agrees
      on them with the team as an experiment, shows the data before and after, and shields the team from the
      pressure to "start just one more". Weak answers: demand that people work faster, add people, simply forbid
      new tasks without dealing with the causes of blockers, or set a limit that nobody follows.
    linkTitles:
      - "The Kanban Guide (kanbanguides.org)"

      Внутреннее приложение Blazor Web App на .NET 10 использует режим `InteractiveServer` и работает на двух

         Смотреть размер кучи и частоту сборок мусора через `dotnet-counters`, снимать `dotnet-gcdump` при разном

  en:
    title: "An InteractiveServer Blazor app runs out of memory and drops users as sessions grow: what do you do?"
    prompt: |
      An internal Blazor Web App on .NET 10 uses the `InteractiveServer` render mode and runs on two instances
      behind a load balancer with session affinity. With about a hundred concurrent users there were no problems.
      After several departments joined, the number of concurrent sessions grew tenfold and more: process memory
      grows to the container limit, the instance restarts, and every user on it sees a lost-connection message and
      loses unsaved data.

      The team added a third instance and at the same time switched the load balancer to round robin. Since then
      some users see that the connection is not restored and they have to reload the page.

      How do you find the cause and what do you fix?
    hint: |
      What does the server keep for every user between two clicks, and what happens to it when the user closes
      the tab or loses the network?
    answer: |
      1. **Understand the model.** Every browser tab of a user is a circuit: instances of all components, their
         fields and scoped services live in server memory while the circuit is alive. After the connection drops,
         the circuit is retained for a while so the user can reconnect. So memory is the number of circuits
         multiplied by the memory of one circuit, plus leaks.
      2. **Measure.** Count opened, connected and disconnected circuits with your own `CircuitHandler`
         (`OnCircuitOpenedAsync`, `OnCircuitClosedAsync`, `OnConnectionUpAsync`, `OnConnectionDownAsync`).
         Watch heap size and GC frequency with `dotnet-counters`, take `dotnet-gcdump` snapshots at different user
         counts and compare which types grow. Divide heap size by the circuit count and check whether memory drops
         after users leave: if it does not, it is a leak, not load.
      3. **Shrink per-circuit state.** Do not keep whole result sets in component fields and scoped services: use
         paging, `Virtualize` and projections into small DTOs. Instead of a scoped `DbContext`, which in server-side
         Blazor lives for the whole circuit and accumulates tracked entities, use `IDbContextFactory<TContext>` and
         a short-lived context per operation. Keep shared reference data once in a size-limited singleton cache
         instead of copying it into every circuit.
      4. **Remove leaks.** Unsubscribe from singleton service events in `Dispose`, dispose
         `DotNetObjectReference` instances, timers and `CancellationTokenSource` objects: otherwise components
         outlive their circuit.
      5. **Tune retention of disconnected circuits.** `DisconnectedCircuitMaxRetained` and
         `DisconnectedCircuitRetentionPeriod` of `CircuitOptions` are set in
         `AddInteractiveServerComponents(options => ...)`. Lower values save memory, but users on unstable
         networks lose state more often.
      6. **Create fewer circuits.** Serve pages that need no interactivity with static server-side rendering
         (static SSR): no circuit is created for them.
      7. **Scale out correctly.** A circuit lives on one instance, so several instances need sticky sessions (or
         Azure SignalR Service with `ServerStickyMode.Required`). Round robin sends connection and reconnection
         requests to an instance that does not have the circuit, which explains the failed reconnects. Use a load
         test to find how many circuits one instance can hold, and scale on memory and circuit count.
    explanation: |
      The key difference of `InteractiveServer` from WebAssembly and static rendering is that user state is kept
      on the server. Memory grows not with the number of requests but with the number of circuits alive at the
      same time and with how much each of them holds. That is why you need numbers first: circuit count and memory
      per circuit. They tell you what to do - shrink state, hunt a leak or add instances.

      Disconnected circuits also take memory: by default the server retains up to 100 disconnected circuits for up
      to 3 minutes so users can reconnect without losing state. When many connections drop at once, that is a
      noticeable amount. A restart caused by running out of memory is especially painful: all circuits of the
      instance are lost at once, users reload their pages and create new circuits on the remaining instances,
      which increases the load there.

      Azure SignalR Service takes connection handling off the app, but not the circuits: components and their
      state still live in the memory of the app instance. If per-user state is still large after optimization and
      there are many users, move interactive parts to `InteractiveWebAssembly`, where state lives in the browser.
      This applies to Blazor Web Apps since .NET 8 and holds for .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "Host and deploy ASP.NET Core server-side Blazor apps"
      - "ASP.NET Core Blazor hosting models"
      - "ASP.NET Core Blazor SignalR guidance"

      4. **Клиентская реализация.** `ClientOrderService` в клиентском проекте вызывает веб-API через `HttpClient`
         (`GetFromJsonAsync`). Она регистрируется в `Program.cs` клиента вместе с `HttpClient`, у которого
         `BaseAddress` указывает на адрес приложения.
      5. **Конечная точка API.** Сервер публикует endpoint (minimal API или контроллер), который делегирует той же
         серверной реализации, чтобы логика запроса была в одном месте.
      6. **Безопасность.** Endpoint доступен любому, кто знает URL, поэтому аутентификация, авторизация и проверка,
         что пользователь получает только свои заказы, выполняются на самом endpoint. В клиентском проекте нет строк
         подключения и секретов: его сборки скачиваются в браузер.
      7. **Двойная загрузка.** Данные, загруженные при пререндеринге, иначе загрузятся ещё раз при переходе в
         интерактивный режим. Их переносят через `PersistentComponentState` (в .NET 10 также декларативно, атрибутом
         `[PersistentState]`) или отключают пререндеринг для этого компонента.
    explanation: |
      Главная особенность `InteractiveAuto` в том, что один и тот же код компонента выполняется в двух разных средах:
      на сервере с полным доступом к базе и в браузере, где доступна только сеть. Интерфейс с двумя реализациями
      переносит выбор среды из компонента в DI: каждый `Program.cs` регистрирует свою реализацию, а компонент об
      этом не знает. Ветвиться по `RendererInfo.Name` внутри компонента не нужно.

      Почему простые варианты не подходят:

      - `DbContext` прямо в компоненте не заработает в WebAssembly: браузер не может открыть соединение с SQL Server,
        а строка подключения попала бы в скачиваемые сборки.
      - Если зарегистрировать сервис только в клиентском проекте, упадёт серверная сторона: при пререндеринге и в
        режиме Interactive Server контейнер сервера не найдёт реализацию интерфейса.
      - Вариант «везде `HttpClient`» работает, но на сервере приложение вызывает само себя по HTTP: лишний сетевой
        переход, нужен абсолютный базовый адрес, а cookie аутентификации пользователя в такой запрос автоматически не
        попадают, потому что серверный `HttpClient` - не браузер.

      `IDbContextFactory<T>` нужен потому, что в режиме Interactive Server scope живёт столько же, сколько circuit:
      scoped `DbContext` держался бы долго и мог бы использоваться одновременно из нескольких обработчиков, а
      `DbContext` не потокобезопасен. Обе реализации должны одинаково вести себя при ошибках, отмене и постраничном
      выводе, и это стоит проверить тестами для каждой из них.

      Режимы отрисовки появились в .NET 8, описанное поведение верно для .NET 10.

      - "Режимы отрисовки Blazor"
      - "Вызов веб-API из Blazor"
  en:
    title: How do you design data access for a Blazor component in the InteractiveAuto render mode?
    prompt: |
      A Blazor Web App on .NET 10 has an `Orders` page with the `@rendermode InteractiveAuto` directive. It must
      show the orders of the signed-in user, which are stored in SQL Server and read through EF Core.

      How do you design data access for this component so that it works everywhere it can run? Explain which
      project holds each piece and why.
    hint: "Where does the code of this component physically run on the first and on later visits, and what is available in each of those places?"
    answer: |
      1. **Know where the code runs.** With `InteractiveAuto` the component first runs interactively on the server
         (in a circuit) while the WebAssembly files download in the background and are cached. On later visits a new
         instance is created in WebAssembly in the browser. A component already rendered never changes its mode.
         The component is also prerendered on the server by default. So it lives in the `.Client` project and cannot
         reference a `DbContext` or other server code.
      2. **Depend on an interface.** The component injects `IOrderService` with methods such as
         `Task<IReadOnlyList<OrderDto>> GetMyOrdersAsync(CancellationToken)`. The interface and the DTOs are declared
         in the client project or in a shared library. DTOs cross the boundary, not EF Core entities.
      3. **Server implementation.** `ServerOrderService` in the server project reads the database directly through
         EF Core, preferably with `IDbContextFactory<T>` and a short-lived context per operation. It is registered
         in the server `Program.cs` and serves both prerendering and the Interactive Server mode.
      4. **Client implementation.** `ClientOrderService` in the client project calls a web API through `HttpClient`
         (`GetFromJsonAsync`). It is registered in the client `Program.cs` together with an `HttpClient` whose
         `BaseAddress` points to the app.
      5. **API endpoint.** The server exposes an endpoint (minimal API or controller) that delegates to the same
         server implementation, so the query logic lives in one place.
      6. **Security.** Anyone who knows the URL can reach the endpoint, so authentication, authorization and the
         check that users get only their own orders happen on the endpoint itself. The client project holds no
         connection strings or secrets: its assemblies are downloaded to the browser.
      7. **Double loading.** Data loaded during prerendering would otherwise be loaded again when the component
         becomes interactive. Carry it over with `PersistentComponentState` (in .NET 10 also declaratively with the
         `[PersistentState]` attribute) or disable prerendering for this component.
    explanation: |
      The key property of `InteractiveAuto` is that the same component code runs in two different environments: on
      the server with full access to the database, and in the browser where only the network is available. An
      interface with two implementations moves the choice of environment from the component into DI: each
      `Program.cs` registers its own implementation, and the component does not know which one it gets. There is
      no need to branch on `RendererInfo.Name` inside the component.

      Why the simple options fail:

      - A `DbContext` used directly in the component cannot work in WebAssembly: the browser cannot open a
        connection to SQL Server, and the connection string would end up in the downloaded assemblies.
      - If the service is registered only in the client project, the server side breaks: during prerendering and in
        the Interactive Server mode the server container finds no implementation of the interface.
      - "`HttpClient` everywhere" works, but on the server the app calls itself over HTTP: an extra network hop, an
        absolute base address is needed, and the user's authentication cookie is not added to that request
        automatically, because a server-side `HttpClient` is not a browser.

      `IDbContextFactory<T>` matters because in the Interactive Server mode a scope lives as long as the circuit: a
      scoped `DbContext` would live for a long time and could be used concurrently by several handlers, while
      `DbContext` is not thread-safe. Both implementations must behave the same on errors, cancellation and paging,
      which is worth covering with tests for each of them.

      Render modes appeared in .NET 8, and the behaviour described here holds for .NET 10.
    linkTitles:
      - "Render modes in ASP.NET Core Blazor"
      - "Call a web API from ASP.NET Core Blazor"

        создаёт новый circuit с новыми экземплярами компонентов и scoped-сервисов. Состояние в памяти потеряно.
        Остаётся только то, что хранится вне circuit: cookie аутентификации (поэтому пользователь остаётся
        залогинен, а корзина пропадает), URL, хранилище браузера, база данных.
      - **Новая вкладка.** У неё свой circuit и свои экземпляры scoped-сервисов, вторая вкладка не видит
        состояния первой.
      - **Разрыв сети.** При коротком разрыве клиент переподключается к тому же circuit, и состояние
        сохраняется. Но сервер держит отключённый circuit ограниченное время и в ограниченном количестве
        (`CircuitOptions.DisconnectedCircuitRetentionPeriod` и `DisconnectedCircuitMaxRetained`, по умолчанию
        3 минуты и 100 circuit) и может освободить его раньше при нехватке памяти. После этого переподключиться
        нельзя, пользователю предлагают перезагрузить страницу, и создаётся новый circuit. Так же circuit
        теряется при перезапуске процесса, развёртывании или выходе сервера из балансировки.
      - **Куда переносить, по вопросу «кто и как долго должен видеть это состояние»:**
        - URL (маршрут, query string): навигационное состояние - фильтры, сортировка, номер страницы, выбранная
          вкладка. Переживает перезагрузку, переносится в новую вкладку вместе со ссылкой, им можно поделиться
          (`[SupplyParameterFromQuery]`, `NavigationManager`).
        - `sessionStorage` через `ProtectedSessionStorage`: привязан к вкладке, переживает перезагрузку, но не
          общий для вкладок. Подходит для черновика формы в одной вкладке.
        - `localStorage` через `ProtectedLocalStorage`: общий для всех вкладок одного origin и переживает
          перезапуск браузера, но остаётся на одном устройстве.
        - База данных на сервере: всё ценное и то, что должно пережить смену устройства или браузера,
          например корзина авторизованного пользователя или сохранённые черновики. Ключ - пользователь, а не circuit.
        - Поля и scoped-сервисы остаются для временного состояния интерфейса, которое не жалко потерять, и как
          кэш поверх надёжного хранилища.
      - **Ограничения.** `ProtectedLocalStorage` и `ProtectedSessionStorage` асинхронны, работают только при
        серверной интерактивной отрисовке и недоступны во время пререндеринга, поэтому их читают в
        `OnAfterRenderAsync` и показывают состояние загрузки. Статическое поле или singleton - не решение: они
        общие для всех пользователей и тоже пропадают при перезапуске сервера.
    explanation: |
      Circuit - это единица интерактивной сессии в режиме `InteractiveServer`. Перезагрузка или новая вкладка - это
      новый HTTP-запрос и новое соединение SignalR, и фреймворк не связывает их со старым circuit: к прежнему
      circuit может вернуться только тот же экземпляр страницы, который продолжает работать в браузере после
      разрыва. Поэтому всё, что лежит только в памяти circuit, по сути является кэшем с временем жизни вкладки.

      Отсюда правило выбора хранилища. Состояние, которое описывает, что пользователь видит, кладут в URL: оно
      переживает перезагрузку и копируется ссылкой. Состояние одной вкладки, которое жалко потерять при F5, - в
      `sessionStorage`. Состояние устройства, общее для вкладок, - в `localStorage`, учитывая, что вкладки могут
      перезаписывать его друг у друга. Всё, что имеет ценность для бизнеса, - в базу. Защищённое хранилище
      браузера шифрует данные через ASP.NET Core Data Protection, поэтому пользователь не может их подменить, но
      объём ограничен браузером, а сами данные остаются на устройстве.

      В многосерверном развёртывании circuit живёт на одном сервере, поэтому нужны sticky sessions, а отказ
      сервера уничтожает все его circuit. В .NET 10 появилось сохранение состояния circuit: объявленное для
      сохранения состояние компонентов (через `[PersistentState]`) может быть восстановлено, когда пользователь
      возвращается после вытеснения отключённого circuit. Это сужает проблему долгого разрыва, но не заменяет
      надёжное хранилище: сохраняется только явно объявленное состояние, ограниченное время, и оно не делает
      состояние общим между вкладками. Описание относится к Blazor Web App начиная с .NET 8 и верно для .NET 10.
